Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi et ath-Tha'alibi transmettent un récit de Ka'b al-Ahbar sur le rugissement de la Géhenne et la parole d'Abraham, ainsi qu'un récit d'Ibn Abbas sur le dialogue entre l'âme et le corps illustré par l'aveugle et le paralytique, que al-Alusi juge peu probable. Sur la grammaire, al-Tabari note l'accord au féminin du verbe avec le mot âme, expliqué par le sens de « chacun », tandis que d'autres y voient une faute. Ar-Razi et az-Zamakhshari distinguent le premier « nafs » (la personne entière) du second (l'individu lui-même).

Ce verset propose une parabole : une cité qui jouissait de sécurité et de tranquillité, où affluaient ses subsistances en abondance de toutes parts, a renié les bienfaits de Dieu, et Dieu lui a alors fait goûter le vêtement de la faim et de la peur, en punition de ses agissements. La plupart des commentateurs, dont Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, identifient la cité à La Mecque et à ses habitants, qui n'étaient pas attaqués et dont les fruits de toutes choses étaient apportés. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir précisent que l'ingratitude consistait à traiter le Prophète de menteur, que la faim dura sept années jusqu'à ce qu'ils mangent du 'ilhiz et des charognes suite à son invocation, et que la peur venait des expéditions du Prophète qui les cernaient. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi entendent l'ingratitude comme l'abandon de la reconnaissance et de l'obéissance, et rappellent que la parabole peut viser une cité non nommée ; al-Razi estime même que la cité visée n'est probablement pas La Mecque elle-même, mais une autre cité prise comme exemple pour elle. Une autre opinion, rapportée par Hafsa dans la transmission de al-Tabari et par Ibn al-Jawzi, identifie la cité à Médine lors du meurtre de 'Uthman ; Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Samʿani et al-Suyuti jugent cette lecture faible ou limitée à l'exemple, et plusieurs y voient une parabole valable pour toute cité semblable. Les lecteurs divergent sur « wal-khawf » : la majorité le lit au génitif, par coordination avec la faim, tandis qu'Abu 'Amr le lit à l'accusatif, par coordination avec le vêtement. Tous s'accordent à voir dans « faire goûter » et « vêtement » des métaphores, la faim et la peur enveloppant le corps comme un habit. Le passage est un avertissement contre l'ingratitude envers les bienfaits divins et contre le rejet du messager.

Ce verset affirme qu'un messager issu de la cité elle-même, dont les habitants connaissent la lignée et la sincérité, leur est venu, qu'ils l'ont traité de menteur, et que le châtiment les a saisis alors qu'ils étaient injustes, c'est-à-dire associateurs et ingrats envers les bienfaits de Dieu. La plupart des commentateurs, dont Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi, identifient la cité à La Mecque et le messager au Prophète Muhammad, et voient dans le châtiment la famine que le Prophète aurait appelée sur eux, à laquelle al-Razi et al-Qurtubi ajoutent parfois la mort au combat de Badr. Al-Tabari et al-Baghawi rapportent ce sens, tandis qu'Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari considèrent que la cité n'est pas nommément désignée et que la parabole sert d'avertissement à La Mecque comme à toute autre cité jusqu'au Jour de la résurrection. Al-Tabari transmet un récit de Hafsa, épouse du Prophète, qui disait qu'il s'agissait de Médine ; Ibn 'Atiyya explique qu'elle voulait dire que Médine avait subi le même sort que l'exemple. Al-Shawkani juge la seconde lecture plus solide, car l'indétermination du mot « cité » porte à la généralité. Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans le verset suivant un passage vers l'ordre donné aux croyants de manger des biens licites et de remercier Dieu, la particule « fa » marquant ce lien. Ils expliquent aussi que l'expression « vêtement de faim et de peur » est une métaphore, qu'al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari analysent en détail, et qu'Ibn 'Ashur y voit un châtiment de portée générale.

Le verset ordonne aux croyants de manger ce que Dieu leur a accordé, licite et bon, et de remercier Dieu pour ce bienfait, s'ils L'adorent véritablement. Ibn Kathir explique que Dieu seul accorde la subsistance et mérite donc seul l'adoration, et que le licite s'oppose à ce qui nuit à la religion et à la vie. Ibn Sa'di précise que la nourriture doit être licite et bonne, ni interdite ni acquise par la spoliation, et consommée sans excès ; la gratitude consiste à reconnaître le bienfait dans le cœur, à louer Dieu et à employer ses dons dans l'obéissance. Al-Baydawi et al-Jaza'iri concrétisent ce remerciement par l'adoration et l'abstention de ce qui est interdit. Al-Zamakhshari propose de comprendre la condition comme « si vous Lui obéissez », ou, si votre prétention est juste, « si vous adorez Dieu à travers les idoles qui sont vos intercesseurs ». Les avis divergent surtout sur les destinataires. Selon Ibn al-Jawzi, la majorité y voit les musulmans. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi, suivant Ibn 'Abbas, y voient le butin de guerre, et al-Razi rattache la faim de la parabole au refus de la foi : une fois l'incroyance abandonnée, on peut manger. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi et al-Sha'rawi rapportent un autre avis, selon lequel le Prophète envoya de la nourriture aux polythéistes affamés de La Mecque ; al-Tabari le juge lointain, les versets suivants traitant de l'interdiction de la charogne. Ibn 'Atiyya comprend « bon » comme « agréable », ou comme un renforcement de « licite ». Ibn 'Ashur pense peut-être aux émigrés en Abyssinie, et al-Alusi rapporte qu'il pourrait s'agir des habitants de Médine avertis par l'exemple de La Mecque.

Ce verset énonce que Dieu n'a interdit que quatre choses dans la nourriture : la bête morte, le sang, la chair de porc et ce qui a été immolé au nom d'un autre que Dieu. Celui qui y est contraint par la nécessité, sans transgresser ni excéder la limite de la nécessité, ne commet pas de péché, car Dieu est pardonnant et miséricordieux. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur l'idée que cette disposition relève de la facilité accordée par la religion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi expliquent que la « bête morte » désigne l'animal mort de sa propre mort, et que le verset reprend ce qui a déjà été dit dans la sourate de la Vache. Al-Razi observe que la limitation à ces quatre interdits est affirmée dans des sourates mecquoises comme médinoises. Sur l'expression « sans révolte ni transgression », les avis divergent. La majorité, dont Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Baghawi, y voit le fait de consommer ces interdits alors que d'autres aliments sont disponibles, et de dépasser les limites fixées par Dieu. D'autres comprennent la révolte comme le soulèvement contre le dirigeant ou le brigandage, et la transgression comme le fait de dépasser la satiété de survie vers la réplétion. Ibn 'Atiyya rapporte que Malik autorisait la satiété et la provision. Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et Ibn Kathir rattachent le verset à la condamnation des interdits inventés par les polythéistes. Ibn Kathir et al-Tha'alibi voient dans la cité de l'exemple La Mecque. Abu Hayyan présente plusieurs interprétations de cette cité, tandis qu'Ibn 'Ashur et al-Alusi considèrent que la restriction vise à distinguer le pur de l'impur.

Ce verset interdit de déclarer licite ou illicite quoi que ce soit par la seule parole de la langue en disant « ceci est licite et ceci est illicite », car une telle déclaration est une invention contre Dieu, et ceux qui inventent contre Dieu ne réussissent pas. Les commentateurs expliquent qu'il visait d'abord les Arabes païens qui interdisaient la bahira, la sa'iba, la wasila et le hami, et réservaient aux mâles le contenu des ventres des bêtes. Ibn Kathir, al-Samʿani et al-Baghawi y voient toutefois une règle générale qui vaut pour quiconque institue une interdiction ou une permission sans fondement scripturaire. Tous s'accordent sur le sens du mensonge : attribuer à Dieu une loi qu'il n'a pas édictée. Leur gain en ce monde est court, et leur châtiment douloureux dans l'au-delà, selon al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et le Jalalayn.

Les avis divergent surtout sur la grammaire. Al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i et al-Zajjaj tiennent que « ma » est un nom verbal et que « al-kadhib » est complément de « taqulu ». Al-Zamakhshari, suivi par Ibn Ashur, voit dans la lam de « li-taftaru » une lam de conséquence et non de finalité : l'invention du mensonge résulte de ces propos sans en être le but. Al-Alusi et Abu Hayyan jugent au contraire que la finalité est plausible, les Arabes ayant parfois attribué à Dieu leurs propres usages, comme le dit le verset 137 de la sourate des Bestiaux. Plusieurs lectures existent aussi pour « al-kadhib », traitée comme complément, comme qualificatif ou comme pluriel, sans changer le sens général.

Des savants déduisent de ce verset une prudence dans les fatwas. Abu Nadra disait avoir craint de rendre des avis religieux depuis qu'il avait entendu ce passage, et Malik, rapporté par al-Qurtubi et Ibn al-Arabi, désapprouvait que le mufti dise « ceci est licite et ceci est illicite » dans les questions d'ijtihad, préférant employer « je le déteste ». Ibn Ashur précise que le blâme porte sur la transformation du licite en illicite, et non sur le fait de s'abstenir d'un aliment par dégoût.

Les commentateurs expliquent que « متاع قليل » est l'attribut d'un sujet sous-entendu : le profit que tirent ceux qui inventent des mensonges sur Dieu n'est qu'une jouissance passagère et minime ici-bas, et il leur reste ensuite un châtiment douloureux dans l'au-delà. La plupart s'accordent à voir dans ce verset une mise en garde contre les païens qui déclaraient licite ou illicite selon leur propre avis, en prétendant que Dieu l'avait ordonné, comme la bahira et la sa'iba. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir rapportent ce sens, Ibn Kathir l'étendant à quiconque innove ou interdit sans fondement légal, par simple opinion. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan et Abu al-Su'ud comprennent que ce « profit » désigne les avantages que procurent les pratiques de l'ignorance, tandis qu'Ibn Sa'di et Ibn 'Ashur y voient la jouissance de ce monde. Ibn 'Atiyya explique que le « succès » (falah) peut signifier la survie comme la réussite des entreprises. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan et Ibn 'Ashur font de la particule « liyaftaru » une lam de conséquence plutôt que de finalité. Sur la syntaxe de « al-kadhib », les grammairiens divergent : complément de « taqulu » ou de « tasifu », lecture au génitif ou au nominatif selon les variantes. Al-Qurtubi rapporte qu'al-Nakha'i et Malik évitaient de dire « ceci est licite, ceci est illicite » pour les questions d'interprétation, préférant exprimer une aversion. Ce verset rappelle ainsi qu'attribuer à Dieu une licéité sans preuve revient à mentir sur Lui.

Ce verset explique que les interdits imposés aux Juifs, qui leur ôtaient certaines bonnes choses, étaient une sanction, et qu'Allah ne les a pas lésés en cela : ce sont eux qui se sont fait tort par leur rébellion et leur transgression. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que les interdits rappelés sont ceux mentionnés dans la sourate Al-An'am : tout animal à sabots fendus, et la graisse des bœufs et des brebis, à l'exception de celle portée par le dos, celle des intestins ou celle mêlée à un os, comme le rapportent al-Hasan, 'Ikrima et Qatada. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi y voient une punition pour leur transgression, et leur tort désigne leur désobéissance. Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan y voient une mise en garde contre les innovations des polythéistes, en montrant que la loi juive comportait elle-même des interdits propres aux Juifs. Ibn 'Ashur note que ces interdits ne figuraient pas dans la loi d'Abraham. Al-Shanqiti et al-Sha'rawi affirment qu'il s'agit d'une sanction propre aux Juifs, et que ces choses étaient licites en elles-mêmes pour les autres. Al-Razi et Abu al-Su'ud y voient une distinction entre cette communauté et les autres, puisque l'interdit ne frappe chez les musulmans que ce qui nuit. Le verset enchaîne sur le pardon accordé à qui commet un mal par ignorance puis se repent et se réforme. La plupart comprennent l'ignorance comme l'absence de connaissance de la gravité de la faute ou la prédominance du désir, tandis qu'Ibn 'Atiyya la comprend comme la transgression délibérée. Aucun de ces commentaires ne conteste que la responsabilité du tort incombe aux Juifs eux-mêmes.

Ce verset annonce que Dieu pardonne et fait miséricorde à ceux qui commettent un mal par ignorance, puis se repentent et s'amendent. Selon al-Tabari, il s'agit de ceux qui ont désobéi à Dieu sans mesurer ce qu'ils faisaient, puis sont revenus à l'obéissance par le regret et le repentir. Al-Mawardi propose deux sens : ignorer que l'acte est un mal, ou savoir qu'il est un mal mais être emporté par le désir, et il ajoute une troisième possibilité, celle de celui qui se hâte d'agir en se promettant de se repentir. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et al-Baydawi expliquent que l'ignorance désigne l'absence de réflexion sur les conséquences, le désir dominant la raison. Ibn 'Atiyya estime que l'ignorance n'est pas ici l'opposé du savoir mais la transgression et l'entêtement, même si l'ignorance au sens de manque de savoir accompagne souvent ces actes. Ibn Kathir rapporte qu'un des anciens disait que quiconque désobéit à Dieu est ignorant. Pour l'ensemble des commentateurs, la réforme (islah) consiste à persévérer dans le repentir et à abandonner la faute. Le pronom « après elle » renvoie au repentir selon la plupart, ou à l'ignorance ou à la faute selon d'autres. Al-Qurtubi rapporte d'Ibn 'Abbas que le mal désigne ici l'association à Dieu, mais la plupart généralisent le sens à toute faute. Ibn 'Ashur voit dans ce verset un apaisement pour les musulmans après la critique des pratiques idolâtres.

Dans ce verset, Dieu loue son ami Ibrahim (Abraham) en le décrivant comme une « communauté » à lui seul, c'est-à-dire un guide accompli dans le bien et un modèle à suivre, puis comme obéissant et dévot envers Dieu, incliné vers la vraie religion et jamais associateur. Les commentateurs y voient une réponse aux Qurayshites, qui se réclamaient de la religion d'Abraham, ainsi qu'aux juifs et aux chrétiens, qui revendiquaient également son héritage.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn Abi Hatim rapportent largement la explication d'Ibn Mas'ud : la « communauté » est celui qui enseigne le bien, et le « dévot » celui qui obéit à Dieu et à son messager. Mujahid, lui, comprend que le mot désigne Abraham seul croyant au milieu d'un monde d'incroyants. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi retiennent que cet homme réunissait en lui des qualités qu'on ne trouve d'ordinaire que dispersées dans une multitude, et al-Baydawi et Abu al-Su'ud suivent cette lecture. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi énumèrent plusieurs sens pour les autres termes : le « dévot » est tantôt celui qui obéit, tantôt celui qui persévère dans l'adoration ou multiplie l'invocation ; le « penchant vers la vraie foi » est rendu par « sincère » chez Muqatil, par « pèlerin » chez al-Kalbi.

Selon les commentateurs, le bienfait accordé ici-bas est compris de plusieurs façons : le bon renom et la langue de vérité (Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid), la prophétie (al-Hasan), l'acceptation par toutes les communautés (Qatada), ou encore une descendance pieuse. Plusieurs d'entre eux, dont al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Shawkani, reconnaissent que ces sens ne s'excluent pas.

Le verset suivant ordonne au Prophète de suivre la religion d'Abraham. Les avis divergent sur sa portée : suivre tout ce qui n'a pas été abrogé, ou seulement les fondements dogmatiques comme le rejet des idoles et l'islam, comme le soutient al-Tabari. Al-Qurtubi juge que la croyance prime sur les règles pratiques, tandis que d'autres citent les rites du pèlerinage.

Cette verse décrit Abraham comme un guide à suivre, rassemblant en lui les qualités du bien, obéissant à Dieu, éloigné du faux pour la vérité, exempt d'associationnisme et reconnaissant envers les bienfaits de son Seigneur. Dieu l'a choisi, élu et guidé vers la voie droite, celle de l'islam fondée sur le monothéisme. Les exégètes s'accordent à voir dans ces qualités la preuve qu'il n'était nullement tel que le prétendaient les Quraych, les juifs ou les chrétiens qui se réclamaient de lui. Ils s'accordent aussi à dire que le mot « umma » désigne ici une personne seule valant une communauté, ou un guide qu'on suit. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn Mas'ud rapportent qu'il s'agit de celui qui enseigne le bien, tandis qu'al-Mawardi et Ibn Atiyya citent d'autres sens, comme l'homme qui était seul croyant à son époque selon Mujahid. Sur le fond, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi et al-Baydawi expliquent la particularité d'Abraham par sa perfection.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu a accordé à Abraham une belle réputation ici-bas et que, dans l'au-delà, il sera parmi les justes. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur ce sens général et divergent surtout sur ce que désigne le bien accordé ici-bas. Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy et al-Alusi y voient un juste renom, une louange durable à travers les âges. Qatada, rapporté par al-Razi et Ibn Kathir, précise que toutes les communautés religieuses l'agréent et le révèrent, tandis qu'Ibn Atiyya y voit son autorité sur l'ensemble de la création. Al-Hasan, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi l'entendent comme la prophétie, alors que Muqatil ibn Hayyan, al-Qurtubi et al-Nasafi la rattachent à la prière des musulmans sur lui dans le tachahhud. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Zamakhshari et al-Shinqiti évoquent une descendance pieuse, et al-Qasimi ainsi qu'Ibn Sa'di réunissent ces bienfaits avec la subsistance, la santé et une vie heureuse. Pour l'au-delà, al-Baghawi affirme qu'il sera parmi les justes avec ses pères pieux au Paradis, tandis qu'Ibn Juzayy et al-Nasafi disent qu'il fera partie des habitants du Paradis. Al-Razi remarque que cette expression n'exclut pas le rang le plus élevé parmi les justes, et il la relie à la demande d'Abraham dans la sourate al-Shu'ara'. Ibn al-Qayyim souligne que la récompense d'ici-bas n'est pas la rétribution complète, réservée à l'au-delà, et al-Sha'rawi affirme que la récompense de l'au-delà est plus grande. Les commentateurs ne contestent pas le sens du verset ; ils divergent surtout sur le sens du bien accordé en ce monde.

Dans ce verset, Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète Muhammad ﷺ de suivre la religion d'Abraham, en étant un croyant pur (hanif), qui se détourne des fausses religions pour le monothéisme, et précise qu'Abraham n'était pas du nombre des associateurs. Les commentateurs considèrent que la « millah » désigne ici les fondements de la foi : le tawhid, le désaveu des idoles et la soumission à Dieu. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Atiyya estiment que cette obéissance porte sur les principes de la croyance et non sur les règles pratiques qui changent selon les époques. D'autres, comme le rapportent al-Razi et Ibn Juzayy, pensent qu'elle englobe toute sa législation sauf ce qui a été abrogé, et al-Mawardi cite un courant chafiite qui retient le même avis ; Ibn 'Ashur, lui, y voit une conformité aux principes de la nature humaine. Al-Sam'ani et al-Razi en tirent qu'un supérieur peut suivre un inférieur, tandis qu'Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi et Abu Hayyan rappellent que le Prophète ﷺ est le plus excellent des messagers. Concernant le hanif, al-Tabari le comprend comme celui qui se détourne des idoles, Ibn 'Atiyya comme celui qui incline vers le bien, et al-Razi rapporte qu'il désigne aussi la circoncision et le pèlerinage. Les commentateurs ajoutent que la phrase sur le sabbat, qui suit, signifie que son observance n'appartenait pas à la religion d'Abraham, mais fut imposée à ceux qui divergèrent à son sujet ; ils s'accordent à dire que Dieu jugera entre eux au Jour de la Résurrection.

Ce verset indique que le sabbat a été imposé à ceux qui s'étaient divisés à son sujet, c'est-à-dire aux Juifs selon la majorité des commentateurs, et que Dieu tranchera entre eux le Jour de la Résurrection sur ce qui les divisait. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn Sa'di s'accordent à dire que le sabbat ne faisait pas partie de la religion d'Abraham.

Les avis divergent sur la nature du désaccord. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi rapportent, d'après Mujahid, Ibn Abbas et al-Kalbi, que Moïse leur avait ordonné d'honorer le vendredi, mais qu'ils choisirent le samedi, jour où Dieu acheva la création ; le sabbat leur fut alors imposé. D'autres, comme al-Tabari qui cite Ibn Zayd, affirment qu'ils ont délaissé le vendredi au profit d'un autre jour. Al-Mawardi énumère trois avis, et al-Sam'ani voit dans le sabbat une malédiction.

Az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Ibn Juzayy et Abu Hayyan proposent une autre lecture : le désaccord portait sur la chasse, qu'ils tantôt autorisaient, tantôt interdisaient, si bien que le châtiment, la métamorphose en singes, les frappa. Qatada rapporte que certains la jugeaient licite et d'autres illicite.

Ibn 'Achur et al-Razi estiment que le verset vise l'opposition aux prophètes plutôt que des divisions entre Juifs, et qu'il répond à la prétention juive d'appartenir à la religion d'Abraham. Al-Qurtubi s'appuie sur le hadith d'Abou Hurayra, qui attribue le vendredi à cette communauté, pour soutenir que Dieu ne l'avait pas fixé explicitement. Enfin, le verset se termine par l'annonce d'un jugement divin qui rétribuera chaque groupe selon ce qu'il mérite.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ d'appeler les hommes à la voie de son Seigneur, c'est-à-dire l'islam, par la sagesse, qui est l'argument juste éclairant la vérité et dissipant le doute, et par l'exhortation excellente, faite de mises en garde, d'encouragements et de menaces. Il doit aussi discuter avec ses contradicteurs de la manière la meilleure, avec douceur et sans brutalité. Le verset se termine en précisant que Dieu connaît mieux que quiconque celui qui s'égare de Sa voie et celui qui est bien guidé, de sorte que le Prophète n'a que la transmission à assurer. Les commentateurs s'accordent pour dire que la sagesse désigne le Coran ou une preuve décisive, que l'exhortation renvoie aux leçons du Coran, à ses ordres et interdits accompagnés d'encouragements et de menaces, et que la discussion la plus belle consiste à faire preuve de ménagement et à éviter l'insulte. Quant à la portée du verset, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Nahhas et Ibn Zayd le tiennent pour abrogé par le verset du combat, tandis que la majorité, dont al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir, le considère comme toujours valable à l'égard des désobéissants parmi les croyants et de ceux dont on espère la foi sans combat. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari rapportent un contexte lié à la bataille d'Uhud et à la mutilation de Hamza, mais la plupart estiment que le verset, mecquois, se rattache à ce qui le précède. Al-Razi et Ibn 'Atiyya relient les trois méthodes aux degrés des hommes : les élites par la démonstration, le commun par l'exhortation, les opposants par la discussion la plus belle. Ibn al-Qayyim y voit le sens correct de la formule.

Ce verset établit que celui qui a subi une injustice peut riposter contre son agresseur par un châtiment semblable à ce qu'il a subi, sans aller au-delà, et que la patience est meilleure pour ceux qui patientent. Les commentateurs ont divergé sur l'occasion de sa révélation et sur sa portée juridique. La plupart, comme al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi, al-Razi et al-Qurtubi, rapportent qu'il fut révélé à propos des martyrs d'Uhud, dont le corps fut mutilé, en particulier Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib. Les musulmans dirent alors qu'ils feraient de même s'ils vainquaient, puis le Prophète ﷺ renonça à cette mutilation et acquitta son serment. Selon Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak et Ibn Zayd, le verset est abrogé par les versets sur le combat, alors que Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, al-Nakha'i et al-Thawri le jugent non abrogé et y voient une règle générale : celui qui a subi une injustice ne doit pas infliger plus que ce qu'il a reçu. Ibn Atiyya et al-Tabari estiment que rien ne prouve l'abrogation. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi insistent sur l'égalité dans la nature et la mesure du châtiment. Al-Qurtubi et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent un désaccord sur la question de savoir si la victime peut prendre sur le dépôt de celui qui l'a lésée : Ibn Sirin et Mujahid l'admettent, Malik le refuse en s'appuyant sur le hadith « Restitue le dépôt à qui te l'a confié ». Ibn Ashur remarque que le premier acte est appelé « châtiment » par allitération. Ibn al-Qayyim discute longuement de la supériorité de la patience, tandis que la plupart des commentateurs précisent que la riposte est permise mais que s'abstenir est préférable, le verset s'adressant aux croyants et au Prophète avec eux.

Ce verset ordonne au Prophète ﷺ de patienter face aux souffrances que lui infligent les incroyants, et les commentateurs précisent que cette patience ne peut venir que du secours et de la grâce de Dieu. L'interdiction de s'affliger sur eux et de se sentir oppressé par leurs ruses signifie, selon eux, que son cœur ne doit pas se resserrer à cause d'eux. La plupart rapportent que la patience visée consiste à renoncer à riposter en représailles et à mutiler les ennemis, comme cela avait été fait aux martyrs d'Uhud, notamment à Hamza. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir désignent les incroyants comme objet de l'affliction, tandis qu'al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Qurtubi admettent aussi qu'il peut s'agir des martyrs d'Uhud. Tous relèvent que « Dieu est avec ceux qui craignent et ceux qui font le bien » signifie une assistance, un soutien et une protection. Sur la lecture de « ḍayq », al-Tabari préfère la forme avec fatha, tandis qu'Ibn Kathir la lit avec kasra, et des lecteurs grammairiens comme Abu 'Ubayda distinguent entre l'angoisse du cœur et l'étroitesse matérielle, alors qu'Ibn Qutayba et al-Farra' les considèrent comme deux formes équivalentes. Al-Razi analyse les causes de la colère, qui sont la perte d'un bien passé et la crainte d'un mal futur, et voit dans le verset une réponse à ces deux causes. Ibn 'Abbas et Ibn Zayd jugent le commandement de patience abrogé par les versets du combat, alors que la majorité le considère toujours en vigueur.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu est avec ceux qui le craignent en évitant ce qu'il interdit, et avec ceux qui font le bien en accomplissant ses obligations. Les commentateurs entendent ici la présence divine comme un soutien, une aide, un secours et une réussite accordée aux croyants, et non comme une présence générale que partage toute créature. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi et al-Sa'di expliquent que la piété consiste à s'abstenir des interdits et que l'ihsan consiste à accomplir les devoirs et à suivre les actes d'obéissance. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan notent que ce verset conclut les versets précédents qui recommandent la justice, la patience et l'appel par la sagesse, et qu'il en constitue la justification. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari distinguent cette présence particulière de la présence générale de la science, de l'ouïe et de la vue. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi comprennent la piété comme le respect de l'ordre divin et l'ihsan comme la compassion envers les créatures. Al-Alusi et Ibn 'Ashur font observer que la première proposition est au passé pour marquer l'acquisition de la piété, et la seconde nominale pour marquer la permanence de l'ihsan. Al-Sha'rawi voit dans l'ihsan une élévation au-delà du devoir, en citant le hadith de Gabriel. Au sujet des versets voisins, certains dérivent une abrogation par le verset du combat, tandis que le plus grand nombre les tient pour clairs et valables.

The commentators explain that "The command of God has come" means that the promised matter is near and certain; the past tense is used to stress that its occurrence is assured. The disbelievers are therefore told not to hasten it, since they were mocking and denying the warning. On what the command refers to, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir, with al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, take it to be the Hour or the punishment of the disbelievers, citing reports about the unbelievers mocking the announcement of the Hour. Al-Tabari prefers that it is a divine threat announcing that punishment is near, since the verse closes with "Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him". Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti follow this reading. Other reports, cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, link the phrase to the punishment at Badr or to the victory of the Prophet. Al-Dahhak understands it as the obligations and legal rulings, but al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya consider this weak, since no Companion is known to have hastened obligations before they were enjoined. Al-Zajjaj sees it as the recompense promised for their disbelief, and Abu Hayyan adds that it may refer to the signs heralding the Hour.

The prohibition "do not hasten it" is understood by most as forbidding them to seek its arrival before its appointed time. Some read the pronoun as referring to God. On the readings, al-Tabari favours the second-person form with the taa, while Ibn Kathir and others note that the transmitted readings differ, and al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud discuss whether the address concerns only the disbelievers or includes the believers too.

God sends down the angels with the Spirit, meaning revelation, upon whomever of His servants He wills, so that they warn people that there is no god but Him and that they should fear Him. The commentators agree that revelation is the core of the prophetic mission and that the message comes down to monotheism and piety. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the Spirit is revelation, which gives life to hearts as the spirit gives life to bodies, while al-Razi links this image to the perfection of the soul, distinguishing theoretical knowledge of God's oneness from practical piety. On what the Spirit is, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and al-Tabari take it to be revelation, al-Hasan and Qatada mercy, Mujahid the created souls, each angel carrying one, al-Zajjaj guidance, Abu Ubayda Gabriel himself, and al-Rabi ibn Anas the Quran. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan also mention Ibn Jurayj's view that the Spirit is a creature in human form, which most judge weak. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Wahidi note the context: the verse answers the mockery of unbelievers who demanded punishment. Readings of the verb vary between shadda and takhfif, without major effect on meaning, according to al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God alone created the heavens and the earth in truth, meaning with wisdom and purpose rather than in vain, and that for this reason He is exalted above what the polytheists associate with Him. Ibn Kathir, al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur note that the particle « bi-l-haqq » expresses connection: creation is tied to a purpose and to wisdom, and truth here is the opposite of futility. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir conclude that the Creator alone deserves worship, since no other can create the heavens and the earth. Al-Razi reads the verse as a refutation of those who claim that the heavens and the earth are eternal, because creation implies coming into being and determination. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also report that « bi-l-haqq » may mean for their eventual end, or to show God's power and His right to command His servants and to raise the dead. Al-Zamakhshari, continuing the passage, describes man, created from a drop and then become a manifest disputer, as one who denies God's favours. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Tabari understand « man » as the whole human species, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers this broader meaning more comprehensive than the occasion of revelation linked to Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The commentators agree that the verse calls for the oneness of God and reflection on creation, and that the exaltation of God above the associators forms its conclusion. They also note that the readings differ between « yushrikun » and « tushrikun », without the core meaning being changed.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds us of God's power in creating man from a humble drop, and that this same being, once fully formed and endowed with reason, becomes a fierce disputant who expresses himself clearly and argues with his tongue. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take "man" to mean the whole human species, and read the verse as an expression of wonder at humanity's ingratitude and its denial of resurrection. Several reports, from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid among others, state that it was revealed about Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, who held a crumbling bone and asked whether God could bring it back to life; al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya nevertheless hold that the verse is general and that this case is included in it. Al-Mawardi and Abu Hayyan distinguish two senses of "disputant": one who argues for himself with clear proofs, and one who disputes with his Creator. Al-Razi and al-Alusi prefer the first, since the context is the proof of the Creator's existence, while others find the second more fitting for censure. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur read it as wonder at the move from a base drop to eloquent speech. The surrounding verses list the benefits of livestock, namely warmth, produce, food, beauty and transport, and commentators such as Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also discuss horses, mules and donkeys. Some jurists take from this that eating horse meat is forbidden, a view the majority rejects, citing other hadiths.

The commentators explain that God created the grazing animals, namely camels, cattle and sheep, for the benefit of mankind. In them there is warmth (dif'), meaning what one is warmed by, such as clothing and blankets made from their wool, hair and fleece, as well as other benefits: offspring, milk, riding and carrying loads, and the meat that is eaten. Most of them agree that dif' means clothing, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan. Az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that placing the prepositional phrase first in 'and from them you eat' shows that eating from these animals is the main way of sustenance, whereas eating other animals, such as poultry or game, is a kind of enjoyment. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand dif' as offspring, which al-Amawi reports from the usage of some Arabs, but Ibn Jarir and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the first meaning the sounder one. Al-Kalbi adds young animals that are not ridden, though no one else adopts this view. The beauty 'when you bring them home in the evening and when you drive them out in the morning' is explained by the fact that they are most splendid on their return, full-bellied and with swollen udders. Ikrima and Ibn 'Abbas take the distant land to be Mecca, while most scholars take it to be any far country; 'except with great hardship' means either fatigue or the loss of half one's strength. Some jurists derive from this verse a prohibition on eating horses, mules and donkeys, while the majority, relying on hadiths reported by Jabir and Asma', hold that the verse does not establish such a prohibition.

This verse in Surat An-Nahl says that God made the grazing animals, camels, cattle and sheep and goats, a source of beauty for their owners. The commentators explain that when the herdsman brings them back in the evening from pasture to their pens, and sends them out again in the morning, the courtyards are adorned by them, their calls echo there, and this delights the household and raises their standing among people. Most of them hold that the beauty is most visible at the return, when the animals come back full-bellied with swollen udders. Al-Zamakhshari gives this same reason for mentioning the return before the outing, and Qatada describes the sight as most wonderful when they come back with large udders and high humps. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the beauty means pleasing appearance and the attention it draws, not beauty in the creatures themselves. The verse goes on to mention the favour of carrying loads to distant lands that people could reach only with great hardship. Most read the word shiqq as hardship, while al-Farra' takes it as half, meaning the loss of part of one's strength. As for the destination, Ikrima, Ibn 'Abbas and others identify it as Mecca, while most scholars take it to mean any distant land. The commentators draw no legal ruling from this passage; some use the following verse to discuss the eating of horses, but that question belongs to another verse.

This verse reminds believers that livestock carry your loads to a distant land that you could not reach without great hardship, and that your Lord is kind and merciful in providing them. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Hasan describe the beauty of the animals when they return in the evening and when they go out to pasture in the morning, their udders full and their humps tall. The commentators agree that camels are chiefly meant for carrying, and that the loads are a traveller's baggage. As for the destination, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima take it to be Mecca, while Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi and others understand it as any distant land. On the phrase 'shiqq al-anfus', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to mean hardship and toil, whereas al-Farra' and others read it as the loss of half one's strength. Abu Ja'far reads the vowel differently, and both forms are recognised as dialects. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss how the beginning and the end of the verse fit together. Some jurists also draw a ruling from the verse about eating horse, mule and donkey meat: Abu Hanifa and Malik see in the mention of riding a sign of prohibition, while al-Shafi'i and most scholars find no prohibition in it and rely on hadiths permitting horse meat.

In this verse God states that He created horses, mules and donkeys so that people may ride them and adorn themselves with them, in addition to their other benefits. The commentators note that the Quranic wording makes riding the main purpose of these animals, with adornment following it. All agree that people benefit from them for riding and carrying loads, but they differ on whether they may be eaten. Ibn 'Abbas, Malik and Abu Hanifa, together with al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna, hold that the verse forbids eating their meat, since God mentioned them for riding and beauty but mentioned livestock for food. By contrast, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and most scholars consider it permissible, arguing that the verse lays down no ruling and only reminds people of God's favours. They cite the hadith of Jabir permitting horse meat and forbidding domestic donkey meat, and the report of Asma' bint Abi Bakr that they slaughtered and ate a horse in Medina. Regarding mules, most scholars regard them as disliked or forbidden. As for the phrase 'and He creates what you do not know', some explain it as creatures unknown to people at the time, others as what God has prepared for the inhabitants of Paradise and Hell, and others give examples such as moths in clothes or worms in fruit. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

This verse states that God has undertaken to show the straight path that leads to the truth, and that some paths deviate from that aim and do not lead the traveller to it. The commentators largely agree on this meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that God must make clear the guidance and distinguish it from error, while Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd specify that this clarification covers what is lawful and unlawful, obedience and disobedience. As for the crooked paths, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak speak of scattered roads and divergent desires, Ibn al-Mubarak and Sahl ibn Abdullah of innovations and deviations, and most scholars identify them with the false religions such as Judaism, Christianity and Zoroastrianism. Al-Tabari and others mention the variant attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ali, 'and among you is one who deviates', which extends the verse to people themselves. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that guiding to the truth is incumbent on God, and that 'had He willed, He would have guided you all' refers to guidance by compulsion; al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Juzayy reject this reading, seeing guidance as demonstration, with God's will following His wisdom. Al-Baydawi, Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi note that the shift in wording between the two parts of the verse serves to distinguish what may be attributed to God from what may not.

This verse recalls the blessing of water sent down from the sky. The commentators explain that God sends down the rain, from which people obtain drink, and through which plants and trees grow in which livestock graze. Nearly all agree that the verb (tusimun) means to pasture one's animals, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari cite Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada and Ibn Zayd to that effect. They note that the root (sawm) relates to a mark, since grazing animals leave traces on the ground. Opinions differ on the meaning of (shajar). For most it denotes any plant growing from the earth, whether or not it has a stalk, while Ikrima, as reported, takes it to mean pasture, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read the preposition (min) as figurative, the vegetation arising from irrigation. Several scholars, including al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur, expand on the list of produce, namely grain, olive, date palm and grape, and present it as a sign for those who reflect. The readings also differ: the majority read (yunbitu) in the third person, while Abu Bakr, transmitting from Asim, reads (nunbitu) in the first person plural. The commentators draw no specific legal ruling from the verse, apart from the report from Ikrima about not selling pasture.

This verse says that God causes grain, olives, palm trees, grapes and every kind of fruit to grow for people through the same water, and that this is a clear sign of His power and oneness for those who reflect. The commentators agree on the plain meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that one water produces many varieties with different tastes, colours and shapes, which proves that the Creator alone deserves worship. The verse ends with the word "reflect" because meditating on plants requires careful thought. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi describe the stages of germination: the seed splits, a stem rises toward the air, roots descend into the soil, and then leaves, flowers and fruit appear. From this they conclude that the variety of fruits, despite the same water, earth and celestial influences, points to a free and wise agent. Ibn 'Ashur notes that attributing growth to God reminds people not to trust their own power alone. On the reading, Abu Bakr, transmitting from 'Asim, reads "nunbitu" in the first person plural, while the majority reads "yunbitu". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that "min kulli" indicates only a part, since the totality of fruits exists only in Paradise, so what grows on earth is a reminder of it. Grain is mentioned first because it is the basis of food. Al-Razi adds that plants for livestock are named before those for people, which he reads as a lesson in good conduct.

This verse recalls God's favour in subjecting the night, the day, the sun, the moon and the stars to human benefit, meaning they are made docile and useful, all by His command. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the night is for rest and the day for earning a living, that the sun and moon serve to mark times, months and years and to order livelihoods, and that the stars guide travellers through the darkness of land and sea. The commentators agree that these are clear signs, for people who use their reason, of God's power and wisdom. The word taskhir is generally understood as making something subservient and beneficial. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the plural 'signs' and the mention of reason are because heavenly phenomena give a more manifest proof of divine power and majesty. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan mention the differing readings: Ibn Amir and Hafs read some of the nouns in the nominative rather than the accusative, which slightly changes the grammatical structure. Al-Razi draws from the passage an argument against the view that worldly events come from the stars or natures alone, and sees in it the proof of a free and wise agent. Ibn Sa'di emphasises that these blessings cover both the interests of this life and those of religion, while Ibn Ashur sees in the verse both a demonstration of divine knowledge and a reminder of favours.

In this verse God tells us that He has made subject to people what He created on earth for them, including animals, plants and other creatures of varied colours, forms and benefits, and that this diversity is a clear sign of the power and oneness of the Creator for those who reflect and remember. The commentators agree that "what He created" refers to the animals, plants and other beings of the earth. The word "colours" is often understood as kinds or species, as al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir do, although some, such as al-Alusi, keep the literal sense of colour. Al-Razi draws from the diversity of colours an argument that the cause of these effects is a free chooser rather than nature, since nature acts uniformly on all parts of a thing while the effects differ. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi see in it the work of a wise Creator. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the reminder concerns what people already know but have forgotten. Scholars differ on the meaning of "remembering": for some it means taking lessons and being admonished, for others it means recalling the basic knowledge that has been neglected. Ibn Sa'di stresses that the mind must call to memory what leads to knowledge, and al-Sha'rawi links the verse to the broader call to observe the created world.

This verse reminds us that God made the sea subservient to His servants: they may eat its fresh flesh, extract ornaments such as pearls and coral, see ships cleave the waves, and seek provision through trade and God's bounty, so that they may give thanks. The commentators agree that the « fresh flesh » is fish, the ornament is pearl and coral, and seeking His bounty means trade. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, along with Mujahid, take the subjugation of the sea to include riding it, diving and fishing. The meaning of « mawakhir » varies. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as ships running, al-Hasan as laden ships, Qatada as ships moving forward and back with one wind, and Mujahid as ships cutting through the wind, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash describe ships slicing the water with their prows. Al-Tabari notes that « makhr » in Arabic means the sound of blowing wind, whereas others take it as cutting the water. On whether eating fish breaks an oath not to eat meat, Malik and al-Thawri hold that it does, while Abu Hanifa holds that it does not, relying on common usage; Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi report both positions. On men wearing pearls, al-Razi and Abu Yusuf hold that they count as adornment, whereas Abu Hanifa holds that pearls alone are not called jewelry in custom. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur also note disagreement over zakat on jewelry without settling it. Overall, the commentators see the verse as a list of blessings calling for gratitude.

The commentators explain that God set firm mountains on the earth so that it would not sway and shake its inhabitants, made rivers flow in it, and laid out roads so that people could reach their destinations. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that when the earth was created it began to tremble, and God steadied it with mountains; this account is attributed to Qatada, al-Hasan, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Wahb ibn Munabbih. They agree that the verb alqa here means place or create, and that the rivers and roads are linked to the mountains by the same act. On the phrase 'an tamid bikum', the scholars differ only in grammar: the Kufans read it as 'lest it sway', the Basrans as 'lest it sway' with an implied 'dislike of', and the meaning is the same.

The commentators differ more on the signs and the star. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take the signs to be landmarks on the road and the star to be a guide at night, while Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Kalbi take the signs to be mountains, and al-Sudi names the Pleiades, the Plough, the two Guards and the Pole Star. The majority holds that the guidance is for travel, while others take it to mean finding the qibla. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi observe that such guidance applies on land and at sea alike. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by Ibn Juzayy, holds that the shift to the third person addresses the Quraysh, who were known for their journeys.

This verse recalls that God set firm mountains on the earth so that it would not sway with its people, made rivers and paths flow through it, and then mentions landmarks and the stars by which travellers find their way. Commentators differ on what the landmarks are. Ibn 'Abbas understands them as road markers by day, al-Kalbi as the mountains, while Mujahid, Qatada and al-Nakha'i take them to be the stars, since some serve as guides and others only as signs. As for the word for star, most exegetes read it as a generic noun for the stars, whereas as-Suddi and al-Farra' specify the Pole Star, the Pleiades, the Great Bear or the Ursa Minor. A hadith transmitted through Ibn 'Abbas identifies the star as the Pole Star, but several commentators regard its authority as weak. On the purpose of guidance, al-Tabari and the majority take it to mean guidance on journeys, while others take it to mean finding the qibla. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that the pronoun refers particularly to the Quraysh, known for their trade journeys and their skill at navigating by the stars, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya argues the wording covers any sign that gives direction. The commentators agree that the verse presents these as divine favours that call for gratitude.

This verse in Surah an-Nahl states that Allah is the Creator who brings all things into being and governs them, while the idols worshipped by the polytheists create nothing and hold no power to harm or benefit their worshippers. How then can they be placed on a par with the One who created these wonders? The verse closes with a rebuke: will you not remember? That is, you should recall the truth and abandon associating partners with God. The commentators agree that the target of the verse is the idols, and that the word (man), normally used for rational beings, is used either because the pagans named the idols gods and treated them as rational beings, or for the sake of matching the preceding phrase, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi explain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi present the verse as a refutation of idol worship. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the logic of the argument would normally have reversed the terms, since the polytheists placed the created on the level of the Creator, so the verse's wording condemns them more sharply. Al-Razi and several Mu'tazilites note that the verse does not settle whether humans create their own acts, and al-Razi finds its use by some Ash'arite theologians unconvincing. The following verse speaks of Allah's countless blessings, and of His forgiveness of those who fall short in thanking Him, especially when they repent and turn back to Him, as al-Tabari explains.

This part of the verse states that God's blessings are too numerous to be counted, so people cannot enumerate them, let alone give thanks for them as they deserve. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir take the meaning to be that people cannot fulfil the true gratitude owed for these blessings. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read it as saying that people cannot fix their number, so that what has been listed is only part of an unlimited whole. Al-Mawardi gives two senses of the verb: to keep count of the blessings, as al-Kalbi said, or to thank God for them, a view reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

The commentators agree on the closing words: God forgives the shortfall in gratitude and shows mercy. Al-Tabari adds that this forgiveness applies to those who repent and turn back to obedience. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that God accepts little thanks despite the abundance of His favours. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud link this passage to the verse in Surat Ibrahim that describes man as wrongdoing and ungrateful, which gives the divine mercy a deeper meaning.

Al-Razi notes that detailed knowledge of all the blessings is beyond human capacity, so one should thank God for the whole as well as for the parts. Al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur also point out that the verse warns the polytheists while leaving them room to repent.

This verse states that God knows what people conceal in their hearts and what they reveal through their words and deeds, and that He will call them to account on the Day of Resurrection. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, agree that it means complete knowledge of both secret and public matters. Many read it as a warning to the disbelievers and to those who worship other than God. Most link this knowledge to the preceding verses on creation and blessings: the One who creates and bestows favours is the One who knows everything, unlike the idols, which create nothing and know nothing. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi connect the sentence to what precedes it, explaining that God forgives human failure to give thanks for His blessings because He knows people's inner state. Ibn 'Ashur notes that placing the subject first implies exclusivity: God alone possesses this knowledge, not the idols. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan mention that the Quraysh were plotting in secret against the Prophet, giving the verse the force of a threat. On recitation, Hafs reads both verbs in the third person, while most readers use the second person; this difference does not change the core meaning. The commentators do not choose between these readings and explanations, presenting them as possibilities within a single context.

This verse states that the idols the polytheists worship besides Allah cannot create anything, and that they themselves are created, so they do not deserve worship. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that the verse refers to the idols and denies them the attributes of divinity by stating their opposites: they are lifeless objects that neither hear nor see and do not know when the resurrection will take place. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read the phrase 'dead, not alive' as a plain description of their inanimate nature. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur also see irony aimed at the polytheists: if their gods do not know when their worshippers will be raised, how could they grant them any reward? Al-Razi notes that the repetition of 'dead' and 'not alive' addresses very ignorant listeners, and he offers another reading in which those invoked are the angels, whom some people worshipped. The verb 'they are created' may mean that Allah created them, or that people carve and shape them; on this second reading, as al-Zamakhshari argues, the idols are weaker than their worshippers. The readers differ over the verb 'invoke', with Asim and Ya'qub reading it with a yā'. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the sentence links the denial of resurrection with the denial of God's oneness. The commentators agree on the central point: whoever creates nothing and knows nothing cannot be a god, and Allah alone is the Creator who knows all.

The commentators explain that God describes the idols worshipped besides Him as unable to create anything, since they are themselves created, and as dead things without souls, unable to hear, see or understand, and ignorant of when they will be raised. How could one worship what is lower than the worshippers, who are alive? On the phrase 'dead, not living', most commentators agree that these are inanimate objects that can never receive life. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read it this way, and Ibn Kathir draws from it that hope for benefit or reward belongs only to the One who knows all and creates all. Al-Samani and al-Zamakhshari explain that 'not living' either reinforces the point or distinguishes these idols from living bodies that once lived or may yet live, such as embryos or animal corpses. The reference of the pronoun in 'they will be raised' is disputed. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan apply it to the worshippers, a mockery of the polytheists whose gods do not know when their followers will be raised. Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, holds instead that God will raise the idols, give them spirits, and that they will disown their worshippers before both are sent to Hell. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy also allow that the pronoun refers to the disbelievers themselves. Al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur note that not knowing the time of resurrection shows that resurrection is bound up with moral responsibility. All agree that the verse denies divinity to the idols.

This verse states that the one true God is the only deity worthy of worship, and it describes those who do not believe in the Hereafter as having hearts that deny this oneness and as being arrogant toward the truth. The commentators treat it as the conclusion of the argument against idol worship that precedes it. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the denial concerns God's oneness and comes with arrogance toward worshipping Him alone, and al-Tabari links it to the attachment of the ancestors to polytheism. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that someone who does not believe in the afterlife does not seek proof or reflect on what he hears, while the believer examines what he is told. Ibn 'Ashur observes that denying the resurrection produces a habit of ignoring consequences and is the root of rejecting revelation. Ibn 'Atiyya considers disbelief in the Hereafter the highest degree of unbelief, since it combines denying God and denying resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the closing threat first targets the polytheists, but its wording applies to every arrogant person. Al-Qurtubi notes that arrogance is the one sin that cannot be concealed, and he cites a hadith on pride. Al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir see the phrase their hearts deny as a statement of rejection, while al-Shawkani notes that arrogance implies refusing the truth out of disdain. The scholars differ mainly on the meaning of the negation before jarama and on whether the arrogance refers to the polytheists alone or to every proud person.

The commentators explain that God knows what these people conceal and what they openly declare, and that He does not love the arrogant who turn away from the truth. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take this to refer to the polytheists who reject God's oneness and refuse to worship Him alone, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that the warning may cover every arrogant person, these disbelievers included. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that their refusal comes from blind imitation of their forefathers, reluctance to return to the truth, and pride, and al-Baydawi adds that unbelief in the Hereafter keeps a person from seeking proof. Most explain the phrase la jaram as meaning 'truly', though Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some take it to mean 'there is no doubt that', and the grammarians differ on its construction. As to what they conceal, Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Naqqash understand it as their consultations in Dar al-Nadwa on killing the Prophet, whereas most commentators read it as everything they hide or display. Several, including al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, cite the hadith that no one will enter Paradise with an atom's weight of pride in his heart, and al-Qurtubi notes that pride is the one sin that cannot be concealed. On the following verses, al-Tabari reports that Quraysh stationed themselves on the roads to turn people away from the Prophet, calling his message the fables of the ancients. Finally, the commentators agree that whoever leads others astray carries his own burden together with a share of the burden of those he misled.

This verse reports that the unbelievers who deny the Hereafter, when asked what their Lord has sent down, reply that it is merely the fables of the ancients, meaning their tales and falsehoods. The commentators say the questioners may be some of them addressing others, Muslims asking to test them, or pilgrim delegations whom the Quraysh tried to turn away from the Prophet at the approaches to Mecca. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this as a refusal and a denial, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the word for what may be read in the accusative or nominative, and that the answer may be mockery, since they do not accept that anything was sent down at all. Many link the occasion of revelation to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who recited history books and tales such as Kalila wa Dimna and claimed his story was more beautiful than Muhammad's. As for the phrase that they may bear their burdens, most read it as a final consequence rather than a purpose: their saying leads them to bear their full sins on the Day of Resurrection, along with part of the sins of those they misled. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi cite the hadith that whoever calls to misguidance bears the like of the burden of those who follow him, without their burden being reduced. Al-Zamakhshari adds that misleading without knowledge does not excuse the one led astray, since he was obliged to reason for himself. Al-Razi and al-Wahidi differ on the meaning of min, the latter taking it to denote kind rather than part. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of those disbelievers who, when asked about the Qur'an, replied that it was merely the fables of the ancients, thereby turning people away from faith. The phrase "that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection" means they will carry their sins entirely, with nothing lightened, and "and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead" means they will also bear a portion of the sins of those they led astray. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir agree that this refers to the weight of their own sins together with the sins of those who followed them, and many cite the hadith that whoever calls to misguidance bears a like burden of those who follow him, without any reduction in theirs. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that the lam in "liyahmilu" denotes consequence rather than purpose, and that "min" is partitive, whereas al-Razi and al-Wahidi take "min" as indicating kind, so that the leader is punished in a manner equal to each of his followers. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the followers are not excused by their ignorance, since it was incumbent on them to examine and distinguish truth from falsehood. Ibn 'Ashur reads "burden" as a metaphor for a sin that weighs on its doer. As for "without knowledge", some take it as describing the misleaders, who mislead without understanding the consequences, while others take it as describing those misled, who do not realise they are astray. The verse closes with a warning: "Evil is what they carry as a burden!"

This verse says that earlier peoples plotted against the messengers, and God brought their scheme down: their structure was uprooted from its foundations and the roof fell on them, so their own plotting became the cause of their destruction. The plain sense is that of a corrupt scheme that recoils on its authors, and all the commentators agree that the punishment came from a direction they did not expect. On who is meant, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Tabari, followed by most exegetes, identify Nimrod ibn Kan'an, who built a tower to climb to the sky; Ibn Kathir relates the reports about its height and about his end, by a wind, by Gabriel's wing, or by a gnat. Others, such as al-Kalbi, point to Nebuchadnezzar or to the 'partitioners' of Surat al-Hijr. Several, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari, read the image as a parable for the nullifying of the disbelievers' schemes and deeds, with the pillars and roof standing for what they relied upon. Al-Tabari holds that the roof means the upper parts of their houses that collapsed on them, and al-Razi sees the phrase 'from above them' as emphasis showing they were beneath it. The next verse describes their disgrace on the Day of Resurrection, when God asks where His associates are. Commentators differ on 'those given knowledge': Ibn 'Abbas says the angels, Muqatil the recording angels, Yahya ibn Sallam the believers, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jassas take them to be the scholars and prophets who speak the truth.

This verse describes how, on the Day of Resurrection, God will disgrace the disbelievers and ask them where the partners they claimed and fought the believers over are. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir read the question as a rebuke that exposes their false claims. The commentators differ on who answers: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take them to be the angels, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also mention the believers, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Juzayy identify them as the prophets and the scholars of each community who called people to monotheism. They say that disgrace and punishment belong to the disbelievers, which expresses mockery of them and serves as a lesson for whoever hears it. Several scholars connect the passage to the story of Nimrod, whose tower collapsed, as an image of the failure of deception. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress that the words express the reality of the Judgment and should not be narrowed. Ibn Sa'di adds that at death the disbelievers will deny their sins, until their own limbs bear witness against them.

This verse describes the disbelievers who die while still wronging themselves, whose souls are taken by the angels. At the moment of death they submit and deny having done any evil, and God answers that He knows well what they did. The commentators agree that the verse concerns those who stayed in disbelief until death. Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi understand the phrase "yielding peace" as submission and surrender, al-Akhfash takes it to mean reconciliation, and Qatada as humility. Most of them report, on the authority of Ikrima, that the verse was revealed about people of Mecca who professed Islam without emigrating and whom the Quraysh forced out to Badr, where some were killed. Ibn Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as a general statement about all disbelievers. On their claim "we did no evil," al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya see a lie told to save themselves, while al-Razi, al-Alusi and al-Shawkani argue they meant it by their own reckoning and did not regard their deeds as wrong. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi add that the reply "yes indeed" may come from God, from the angels or from the people of knowledge. Ibn Ashur holds that the passage belongs to the unbelievers who died in disbelief and is not a speech of the Day of Resurrection.

This verse says that God tells the wrongdoers, who had denied any evil in their deeds, that they will enter the gates of Hell to remain there forever, and that Hell is a wretched abode for the arrogant who turned away from faith and from worshipping God alone. The commentators agree that the address is to the disbelievers and that the arrogant are those whose pride led them to disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand the gates of Hell as its levels, while most say they are its categories of punishment, and some hold that each group has its own gate. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that this punishment begins at death, when souls enter Hell, and that souls return to bodies on the Day of Resurrection, whereas al-Qurtubi suggests it may be a foretaste of the punishment of the grave. On the phrase 'they offered peace', al-Tabari, al-Akhfash and Qutrub take it to mean submission and reconciliation, Mujahid and Muqatil take it to mean humility, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya link it to a scene of the Last Day in which the disbelievers first deny and then admit their deeds. In the verses that follow, which concern the believers, Ibn 'Abbas explains the good reward as the multiplication of rewards, al-Dahhak as victory, and Mujahid as goodly sustenance. Most commentators take the abode of the Hereafter to be Paradise, while al-Hasan takes it to be this world, where the pious gather provision for the next.

This verse reports that when the pious are asked what God has sent down, they answer "good." The commentators explain that the Quran is good, a mercy and a guidance. The verse then promises the doers of good a "good" in this world and a far better abode in the Hereafter. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this good in this world as an honorable reward, victory and a good provision. Ibn 'Abbas reports it as the multiplication of reward up to tenfold or more, al-Dahhak as victory and conquest, and Mujahid as a good livelihood. As for the "abode of the pious," most exegetes take it to mean Paradise, while al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to mean this world, where the pious gather provision for the Hereafter. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi describe the Gardens of Eden, with rivers flowing beneath and whatever they desire, as the reward of the pious. Regarding those whom the angels take in a pure state, commentators explain purity as freedom from polytheism, good deeds and words, or an easy death. The angels greet them with peace and announce Paradise. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that this greeting comes at death, while Muqatil places it at the entrance to Paradise. Commentators broadly agree on the promise of good in both abodes, while they differ on the meaning of the "good" in this world and on which abode is meant by the abode of the pious.

This verse describes the Gardens of Eden that the god-fearing will enter, with rivers flowing beneath them, where they will have whatever they wish, and this is how God rewards the righteous. The commentators explain "Eden" as a lasting abode, from which there is no departure, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi say. They agree that the verse completes the description of the home of the pious mentioned just before, and that most of them understand the gardens of Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that the grammar of "gardens of Eden" can be read either as a subject with "they enter them" as predicate, or as the announced topic of an omitted subject, without any real change of meaning. They all link "whatever they wish" to the fullness of Paradise, and al-Razi holds that such a state is found only in the hereafter. Most understand the "pious" as those who guard against associating partners with God and against sins. The commentators agree that the pious are those who die in purity, "tayyibin": al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take this as purity from polytheism, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as readiness for death. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report that the angels greet them and announce Paradise, whereas Muqatil and al-Hasan place this greeting at the entrance to Paradis. All accept that good deeds are the cause of entering Paradise, and Ibn 'Atiyya cites a hadith that no one enters by works alone, without the commentators settling between these readings.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the God-fearing at the moment of death: the angels take their souls while they are pure from associating partners with God and from sin, greeting them and announcing that they will enter Paradise because of their good deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi generally agree that "pure" means purity from polytheism and defilement, and that the good news comes at death. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi report that the angel of death conveys the greeting of the Lord to the believer when his soul is taken, a view also cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir from Ibn Mas'ud. As for the meaning of "tayyibin", al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several views: righteousness, faith, purity of words and deeds, a soul at peace and confident in reward, or an easy death. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi transmit these opinions. Al-Zamakhshari understands purity as freedom from wronging oneself through disbelief and sin, since the verse contrasts these righteous people with those who wronged themselves. On the timing of the greeting, most place it at death, while Muqatil and al-Hasan place it at entry into Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, and al-Hasan takes the taking of souls to mean the death of resurrection. Hamza and al-A'mash read the verb with a third-person plural, while the rest read it with a second-person form. On the particle "bima" in "for what you used to do", Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Alusi note that deeds are the cause of entry, and that a hadith saying no one enters Paradise by his deeds does not contradict this, since divine grace is the foundation. This point nonetheless remains discussed among the exegetes.

This verse says that the disbelievers are waiting for only one of two things: that the angels come to take their souls, or that the command of your Lord comes, meaning the punishment or the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the angels to be the angel of death and his helpers, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy understand the command of God as the Last Day or a punishment in this world. Al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the coming of the command may be a punishment that uproots the wrongdoers. All agree on the phrase that God did not wrong them: He did not punish them unjustly, since they deserved it, and it was they who wronged themselves through disbelief. Ibn Kathir adds that God had given them warning by sending His messengers and revealing His books. As for the evil deeds that befell them, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir see them as the consequences of their disbelief, Ibn Atiyya extends them to this life and the next, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take them as the requital of their misdeeds. Ibn Ashur sees in the verse a warning against the complacency that delay of punishment can produce among the pagans. The commentators also debated the reading of the verb "come" with a ta or a ya, as recorded by al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi. Ibn Sa'di sums up the meaning by saying that such people repent only when the punishment strikes them.

The commentators explain that this verse describes how earlier peoples who associated others with God and rejected their messengers received the due consequences of their evil deeds, and that the punishment they used to mock enveloped them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others understand the evil deeds as the punishments for their disbelief and sins. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi explain that it means the recompense for their deeds, and that calling the recompense by the name of the deed is a figure of speech, or that a word is omitted. All agree that the destruction of these nations was not an injustice from God, since they wronged themselves through disbelief and rejection of the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the recompense is for their evil deeds, while al-Razi takes the punishment to be for their mockery itself. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur connect the verse to a warning to the Meccan polytheists not to feel secure because the punishment is delayed, and to hasten to faith. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the mockery targeted resurrection, judgment and punishment. The scholars agree on the general meaning, and differ mainly on the wording and on what is implied.

This passage reports the argument of the idolaters who invoked God's will to justify their polytheism and the prohibitions they had invented: had God willed it, they said, neither they nor their fathers would have worshipped anything but Him, nor would they have forbidden anything. Several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Sam'ani, hold that they spoke this sarcastically and not from genuine belief. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy stress that God forbade this shirk, and that the destruction of earlier peoples shows He did not approve of it. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir distinguish between God's all-encompassing decreed will and His legislative will that commands good. Al-Razi reports the Mu'tazilite reading, which sees in the verse proof that God does not prevent anyone from believing and that messengers only convey the message, while the Ash'ari position he defends holds that guidance and misguidance lie with God alone. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that messengers have no duty to compel people. All agree on the general sense: every community received a messenger calling it to worship God alone and to avoid false deities, and some were guided while others remained in error. Ibn 'Ashur explains that this argument amounts to a denial of the messengers, whose task is only clear transmission. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn note that the Prophet should not grieve over those whom God has left astray. The commentators thus reject the excuse of predestination, while differing on the nature of divine will and on the precise meaning of guidance and misguidance.

This verse says that God sent a messenger to every community, telling people to worship God alone and avoid the taghut, meaning whatever is worshipped besides Him. Mankind then divided: some were guided by God and followed the messengers, while others were held fast in error and turned away and denied. The verse then tells the listeners to travel the earth and see the end of those who denied, and it consoles the Prophet ﷺ: he should not grieve over the guidance of his people, since God does not guide those whom He leads astray.

Commentators agree on the core: the message of all prophets is one, namely worshipping God alone and rejecting the taghut. Most understand taghut as anything worshipped other than God, although al-Hasan takes it to mean Satan. They also agree that the fate of the deniers was destruction and the ruin of their homes, and that the journey urged by the verse is meant to draw a lesson from the remains of peoples such as 'Ad and Thamud.

The disagreement concerns guidance and misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari sees guidance as a favour God gives to those He knows to be receptive, and abandonment as the lot of those who persist in disbelief. Al-Razi, defending divine will, holds that God guides and misguides according to His prior decree, and that the command to believe is general while the will to guide is particular. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi place guidance in the human choice to accept what is good, and misguidance in the choice to persist in evil. On recitation, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the form yahdi as meaning yahtadi (to be guided), whereas the majority reading yuhda is taken as 'no one guides him whom God misguides'.

Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi reject the appeal to divine will made by the polytheists to justify their practices, noting that God forbade these practices through His messengers.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that, however eagerly he seeks the guidance of his people, God does not guide those whom He has led astray, and those people have no helpers to shield them from punishment. The commentators agree that guidance and misguidance belong to God alone, and that the Prophet's zeal does not alter the fate of those upon whom error has been decreed. The verse is therefore a consolation for the Prophet, whose duty is only to deliver the message.
