Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that whoever God misguides has no guide, and Ibn Sa'di adds that the Prophet's task is only to convey the message. The scholars differ on how to read the verb. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yahdi, with the yā' open and the dāl kasra, which al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi take to mean that God does not guide whom He misguides; al-Farra' noted that yahdi can also mean yahtadi, to be guided, a sense followed by Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi. The other readers have yuhda, with the yā' vowelled and the dāl open, and al-Tabari prefers this reading, since yahdi in the sense of yahtadi seems rare in Arabic; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim also choose it, and it means that whoever God misguides has no guide. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur report the same reading for Ibn Mas'ud and the Kufans. Al-Razi draws a theological argument from the text in favour of predestination. The commentators do not decide between the readings, but they show that both lead to the same general meaning.

The verse reports that some disbelievers swore by God with the most emphatic oaths that God would never raise the dead. The reply, "Yes" (bala), affirms that He will indeed raise them, as a promise He has made and which is true. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read this as a direct refutation of the deniers. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur take "most people" to mean the unbelievers, while Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Juzayy attribute their ignorance to a failure to grasp that resurrection follows from divine wisdom.

Ibn 'Ashur explains that the deniers thought a decayed body could not return to life. Al-Razi develops this point: what returns after annihilation cannot be the same being, and he answers with two proofs, that God's promise binds Him, and that God's power is not limited by matter. Al-Alusi notes that most theologians reject the claim that re-creating the very same individual is impossible, a view held by the philosophers, and he leaves the question open without choosing between them.

Several commentators give an occasion of revelation. According to Abu al-Aliya, a Muslim who was owed a debt by a polytheist spoke of hoping for resurrection, and the pagan swore that God would raise no one. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also cite Ibn 'Abbas, who rejected the claim of some Iraqis that 'Ali would return before the Day of Judgment, and al-Shawkani regards that reading as false.

This verse explains the wisdom behind the resurrection, as the commentators present it. God raises people so that He may make clear to them the truth about what they disputed, including the resurrection itself, and so that the disbelievers who denied it and swore against it may know that they were liars. Most exegetes connect this verse to the preceding phrase, 'a promise binding upon Him, true': Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi make it the purpose of the resurrection. Al-Tabari instead links it to the statement that a messenger was sent to every community. They agree that the phrase 'so that' depends on an implied resurrection. As for the matter disputed, Qatada takes it to cover all people, Ibn al-Jawzi says it is what believers and polytheists disagreed about, such as monotheism or the resurrection, and al-Razi includes the resurrection itself. Ibn al-Qayyim adds a second wisdom: the falsehood of the wrongdoer is exposed and he is humiliated. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the words 'they were liars' carry a rebuke and an implied threat of punishment. The next verse states that when God wills a thing He need only say 'Be,' and it is, so resurrection is no effort for Him. Readers differ on 'fayakūna': Jumhur read it in the nominative, while Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it in the accusative; most commentators limit themselves to this grammatical point. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya observe that this formula does not imply addressing something not yet existing. In short, the commentators agree that the resurrection is true and consistent with divine wisdom and power, but they differ on the precise subject of the dispute and on how the phrase 'so that' is to be attached.

This verse states that when God wills a thing, He says to it "Be," and it is at once. The commentators draw from it that creating, and raising the dead, costs God no labour or effort. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain that there is no toil or hardship in creating, whether bringing things into being or resurrecting the dead. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read the "saying" as a figure of speech for the speed of realisation and the ease of God's will, since there is no actual speech or listener, and they avoid addressing something non-existent. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn stress that the command needs no repetition and is carried out in a single instance, as other verses also show. Al-Razi cites the verse, as some of his fellow theologians did, as an argument for the eternity of God's speech; he then examines and criticises that argument and holds that the verse indicates the createdness of audible speech. On whether a non-existent thing can be called a "thing," al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn al-Anbari answer that the word refers to what is known to God before creation, as if already seen, while al-Zajjaj treats the lam as causal. As for the reading, the nominative "fayakunu" is that of most readers, meaning "so it is," whereas the accusative, read by Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i, is coordinated with "an naqula." Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse answers the polytheists' denial of resurrection and shows how easy it is for God to re-create.

This verse promises that those who emigrated for God's sake after being wronged will be settled in a good place in this world, and that the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew. The commentators agree that emigration here means leaving one's homeland and kin seeking God's pleasure, and that the wrong refers to the persecution the Muslims suffered in Mecca. The meaning of the good dwelling in this world is explained in several ways: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and Qatada say it is Medina, Mujahid says a good provision, al-Dahhak says victory over the enemy, while others say it is dominion over Mecca and the conquered lands, or a lasting good reputation and honour for their descendants. Ibn Kathir holds that these views do not contradict each other, since God compensated the emigrants for what they left with something better in this life. As to the occasion of revelation, the majority, including Ibn Ishaq and al-Zamakhshari, link it to the emigrants to Abyssinia, while others name Bilal, 'Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab or Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl; al-Tabari holds that it applies to all emigrants in general. Most take the phrase 'if they only knew' to refer to the disbelievers, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi apply it to the emigrants themselves. It is also reported that 'Umar, when giving the emigrants their stipend, would say that what was promised in this world was less than what was stored up for them in the next.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the emigrants who patiently endured the hardship suffered for God's sake and who place their full trust in their Lord alone. The plain meaning is that they bore the injury inflicted upon them and entrusted their affairs to God in times of difficulty. The verse follows the promise made to those who emigrated after being wronged: a good dwelling in this world and a greater reward in the Hereafter. The scholars differ on who is meant. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others identify them as the emigrants to Abyssinia, Dawud ibn Abi Hind links the verse to Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, and al-Kalbi and Abu Salih name Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab and Ammar. Ibn Atiyya considers the majority view the soundest, while holding that the verse includes all emigrants. As for the good dwelling, Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi and Qatada take it to be Medina, Mujahid a good provision, al-Dahhak victory over the enemy, and others conquests or a lasting good reputation for their descendants. Al-Zamakhshari and others report the variant reading of Ali, linthwiyannahum. Al-Razi and others report that Umar would give the emigrants their share while reciting this verse. The pronoun in 'they knew' refers either to the disbelievers or to the emigrants. The following verses state that all messengers were men, and several commentators, including Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan, say the people of the reminder are the Jewish and Christian scholars, while al-Zamakhshari notes the view that they are the people of the Quran.

The verse states that God sent before Muhammad ﷺ only men, not angels, to whom He revealed His message, answering the Quraysh who found it strange that a messenger should be human. They are told to ask the People of the Reminder, whom most commentators identify as the Jews and Christians, to confirm that the earlier messengers were human. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Tabari understand this as the people of the Torah and the Gospel, Mujahid restricting it to the Torah, while al-A'mash and Ibn Uyayna mean those among them who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam. Ibn Zayd takes the Reminder to be the Quran and its people to be the Muslims, while al-Mawardi and al-Zajjaj see them as scholars of past histories. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge that the non-converted Jews and Christians are more likely meant, since their testimony carries weight against the pagans. On the phrase about clear proofs and scriptures, opinions differ: some attach it to the sending, others to an implied verb, others to the revelation. Several scholars, including al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, draw from the verse the duty to ask scholars about what one does not know, and some infer permission for an ordinary person to follow a jurist. Al-Alusi notes that the prevailing view forbids a mujtahid to follow another, while those who reject analogical reasoning rely on this text. The verse ends by stating that the Quran was revealed to explain to people what was sent down to them, so that they may reflect.

This verse states that before the Prophet ﷺ God sent only men, to whom He revealed, and that He sent down to him the Reminder, the Quran, so that he might make clear to people what was sent down to them, and that they might reflect. Most commentators read it as a reply to the Quraysh, who found it hard to accept that a messenger could be a human being, so they are told to ask the people of the Book. Opinions differ on who the 'People of the Reminder' are: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan take them to be the Jews and Christians, Ibn Zayd takes them to be the people of the Quran, and al-Zajjaj takes them to be anyone known for knowledge. Ibn 'Atiyya judges the most apparent reading to be the Jewish and Christian scholars who had not embraced Islam. On the grammar of 'with the clear signs and the scriptures', al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari attach it to 'We sent' within the scope of the exception, while others attach it to an implied verb, 'We sent them'. On the Reminder, al-Mawardi gives two readings, the Quran or knowledge. Mujahid takes the explanation to cover clarifying what is general or difficult, which includes what the Sunna makes clear, while Ibn 'Ashur notes that the explanation is broader than merely stating the intended meaning and includes analogy and inference from the text. As for 'so that they may reflect', Mujahid reads it as 'so that they may obey', but most take it as contemplation and reflection.

This verse rebukes those who plotted evil against the Prophet and his companions, most of whom the commentators identify as the idolaters of Mecca, though Mujahid names Nimrod son of Kan'an. Its tone is a warning posed as a rhetorical question: how can they feel safe from being swallowed up by the earth, as Qarun was, or from a punishment coming upon them from a direction they do not expect? Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the evil deeds as polytheism and sins, while al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take them to mean the punishments that will afflict the plotters. On the phrase about their comings and goings, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada speak of journeys, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj of day and night, and al-Zamakhshari of their trade. The majority, including al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, read the phrase 'by gradual wasting' as a slow reduction of wealth and lives until destruction, supported by a line of pre-Islamic poetry that Umar asked about. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi instead read it as fear, meaning that one group is punished while the rest are terrified. The commentators agree that God's mercy delays the punishment, and they point out that the verse is followed by a passage on the prostration of shadows and of all creation.

This verse warns the Meccan disbelievers who devised evil schemes, including against the Prophet ﷺ, that God may seize them while they are busy moving about and conducting their affairs, and they will not escape Him. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Muqatil take the word taqallub to mean their journeys, while Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak understand it as their coming and going by night and day, and al-Zajjaj as all their changing activities. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi link it to their trade and travels.

On the phrase 'ala takhawwuf, most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand it as a gradual reduction of wealth, people and crops until total destruction. They report that Umar ibn al-Khattab did not understand the word and asked the people, and a man from Hudhayl told him that in his tribe's language it means to diminish, citing a line of poetry by Abu Kabir al-Hudhali. Al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and al-Hasan instead read it as fear: God punishes one group so that the others fear the same fate. Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi mention both readings.

The closing words, that your Lord is kind and merciful, are explained by nearly all as meaning that God does not hasten punishment but grants respite. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the particle inna here expresses causation, giving the reason for what precedes.

This verse states that God is able to destroy those who plot evil, understood by most commentators as the people of Mecca, in whatever way He wills: seizing them while they travel and go about their affairs, or seizing them through a gradual loss called takhawwuf. The commentators differ on the meaning of this last word. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba and most exegetes take it as diminution, a slow wearing away of their wealth, persons and crops until they are wholly destroyed; they cite a line attributed to Abu Kabir al-Hudhali, and report that 'Umar asked the people about its meaning until an elderly man from Hudhayl confirmed it was their dialect. Others, including al-Hasan, al-Baydawi and al-Razi, read it as fear: God destroys one people so that the rest fear, and then seizes them while they already dread punishment. Al-Layth understood haste, and Qatada understood that God may punish or pardon. As for 'in their comings and goings', Ibn Jurayj and others take it as day and night, while Qatada and others take it as journeys for trade. Nearly all agree that the closing words, 'your Lord is most kind and merciful', mean that God does not hasten punishment but grants respite, which gives the repentant time to return.

In this verse God reminds the disbelievers that they have seen how the shadows of the things He created, such as mountains, trees and others, shift to the right and left as the sun moves, and that these shadows submit to God and obey His arrangement, humbled and abased. The commentators explain the verb yatafayya’ (to incline back and forth) as returning, leaning and turning from one side to the other. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Dahhak say that the right refers to the beginning of the day and the left to its end; Ibn Abbas holds that the shadow follows the sun wherever it turns, while al-Kalbi describes a shadow that passes in front of, behind, to the right and to the left of a person over the course of the day. As for prostration (sujjadan), most of the early scholars take it to mean obedience, submission and yielding, whereas Mujahid and al-Dahhak say that the shadows themselves prostrate, their shape resembling that of one who prostrates; al-Hasan said that your shadow prostrates to God while you do not. Ibn Kathir understands that everything with a shadow prostrates through its shadow. The “humbled” (dakhirun) are those who are abased and lowered. Al-Razi explains the masculine plural by saying that abasement is a quality of rational beings. The verse uses the singular for the right and the plural for the left, and the exegetes offer several grammatical reasons for this, including Arabic usage that may keep one form singular, or the fact that a shadow begins as one and then multiplies. The passage aims to unsettle the deniers and remind them of God's power and majesty, and the submission of angels and animals shows how universal this obedience is.

This verse states that everything in the heavens and on earth submits to Allah and yields to His will, including the creatures that move upon the earth and the angels, who never refuse to worship Him. The commentators explain that prostration here may mean voluntary worship, which is rewarded for the one who performs it, or the compelled submission of creatures by their nature and subjection; both are gathered under the idea of submission. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that one term covers both rational and non-rational beings, and al-Nasafi explains that the word used is 'ma' because 'man' would refer only to rational beings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others say the angels are singled out for honour, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi note that some understand them to include Gabriel or the angels of earth. As for the phrase 'above them', most, including al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, read it as the fear of awe and reverence, some take it as the supremacy of divine power, and others as a punishment descending from above. Later exegetes also debated the infallibility of the angels and their rank relative to humans, questions on which the commentators differ. This is a recitation prostration verse.

This verse describes the angels, who fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded. The commentators agree that the angels obey without fault and do not act arrogantly, and that their fear is reverential awe. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the fear as dread of a punishment that might descend from above, while others, such as al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, understand it as awe and majesty. Al-Tabari also reports that the word "wasiban" means constant or lasting, referring to the obedience owed to God.

As for the phrase "above them", al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as God's superiority in power and dominion, not in place. Ibn al-Jawzi records two readings: a punishment coming from above, and a description of His exalted greatness. Al-Sam'ani holds that it is a quality of exaltation belonging to God, without modality. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di stress God's supremacy over all things, while al-Sha'rawi rejects any spatial meaning and understands it as higher rank.

Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the angels' fear, despite their freedom from sin, grows with closeness to God and with knowledge of His greatness. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that the verse shows the angels are under obligation and stand between fear and hope.

This verse commands people not to take two gods, since there is only one God, and so He alone is to be feared. The commentators agree on the central meaning: it rejects association and affirms God's oneness. They differ on the role of the word "two" in "two gods, two". Al-Zamakhshari explains that the number stresses the plurality being forbidden; Ibn 'Atiyya notes it may simply be emphasis, while al-Razi gives a rational argument that duality contradicts divinity. Al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and al-Shawkani treat the shift to the first person in "so fear Me" as a device that heightens the sense of awe.

In the next verse, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the religion, meaning obedience and sincere worship, belongs to God alone. They differ on "wasiban": Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and most exegetes take it to mean "lasting", while Ibn 'Abbas in another report says "obligatory" and al-Farra' says "pure". For "din", Mujahid explains it as sincerity, Sa'id ibn Jubayr as worship, and 'Ikrima as testifying to the oneness of God.

The commentators, following al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, state that all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, that every blessing comes from Him, and that people call on Him in hardship, though some associate others with Him once relieved. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read this as a rebuke of such ingratitude.

This verse states that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, both in creation and in ownership, and that obedience and devotion are His alone, lasting forever. It then asks why people should fear anyone other than Him, since none else can harm or benefit. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, take the word wasiban to mean lasting, relying on Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and on a line of verse by Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali. Ibn Abbas is also reported to have said it means obligatory, a view noted by al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, who argue that every blessing creates a duty of obedience. Al-Farra and al-Kalbi understand it as sincere or pure, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi mention the sense of weariness, meaning obedience remains due even when it is hard. Regarding din, Mujahid says it is sincerity, Ibn Jubayr worship, Ikrima the testimony of faith together with the legal punishments, and Ibn Qutayba obedience, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi allow the sense of recompense. The following verses note that every blessing comes from God and that people call upon Him in hardship, yet many associate others with Him once relief arrives. Commentators differ on the particle in the phrase li-yakfuru: some read it as expressing purpose, others as expressing the eventual outcome. Ibn Kathir reports both readings.

This verse states that every blessing people enjoy, whether health, provision, children or guidance, comes from God alone, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi explain. The hardship (ḍurr) that then touches them is taken by most commentators to mean sickness, drought or poverty, and it drives people to cry out in supplication; the word ju'ār originally means the bellowing of a bull, as al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note. The commentators agree in rebuking those who associate partners with God after their hardship is lifted. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi all express surprise at this. They differ on the particle in 'li-yakfurū': Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read it as expressing purpose, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi also allow that it denotes an outcome. On who the 'group' refers to, Ibn 'Abbas says the hypocrites, Ibn al-Sa'ib the disbelievers, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi debate whether 'min' is explanatory or partitive. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and the authors of the Jalalayn, conclude that the closing command 'tamatta'ū' is a threat, and that people will soon learn the consequences of their conduct.

This verse describes a recurring human pattern: when harm strikes, whether sickness, famine or hardship, people cry out to God alone, but once He removes the harm, a group among them returns to associating others with Him. Al-Tabari explains that this group sacrifices to idols in thanks to whoever they think delivered them, and reads the phrase 'that they may disbelieve' as a threat. Ibn Kathir holds that the lam here may be the lam of consequence, or of purpose, meaning they were allowed to do so in order to deny God's favours. Al-Razi calls this ignorance and error, since human nature recognises in distress that there is no refuge but God, and he recounts witnessing people pray during an earthquake and forget it once it stopped. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take the group to be hypocrites in some reports, while Ibn al-Sa'ib takes them to be disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that 'min' may be explanatory, so that the group is the addressees themselves, or partitive, so that some of them take heed and turn back. Ibn 'Ashur explains that 'thumma' marks a gap in rank rather than in time, and that the phrase 'when' signals the suddenness of the relapse. Al-Alusi and al-Shawkani report the same readings. The verse closes with a warning, which most commentators take as a severe threat, and al-Shinqiti notes that the Qur'an repeats this theme to show how quickly people relapse.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage rebuking those who associate partners with God after He has removed harm from them. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, a group of people, once relieved of illness, famine or hardship, turn to worshipping idols and sacrificing to them in gratitude to someone other than God, who had delivered them. The phrase «li-yakfurū» is taken by most as the lam of consequence, meaning that the outcome of their conduct is ingratitude for the blessing. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Tabari, however, read it as the lam of purpose, namely that they intended by their association to deny the favour and to ascribe it to others. «Fa-tamatta'ū» is a command of threat, and «fa-sawfa ta'lamūn» means that you will come to know the end of your affair.

All agree that the address is to disbelievers or polytheists. Ibn 'Abbas took the «group» to mean the hypocrites, while Ibn al-Sa'ib said it refers to the unbelievers. Al-Razi holds that associating partners after deliverance is ignorance and error, since human nature, in distress, recognises that there is no refuge except God. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the address may be general while the group meant is the disbelievers, with «min» explanatory rather than partitive.

Linguistically, most commentators understand «tajarūn» as raising the voice in supplication and crying for help, from the bellowing of a bull, as Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhshari point out. The exegetes draw no specific legal ruling from this verse; they focus mainly on the warning and the moral lesson it conveys.

This verse describes a practice of the polytheists, who set aside for their idols, which know nothing and can neither benefit nor harm, a portion of the wealth God had given them, using it to draw near to these deities. God swears that they will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about this fabrication against Him. The commentators differ on what the phrase "that which they do not know" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Sam'ani take it to mean the polytheists, who do not know the true nature of these gods and have no proof of their power. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that it may refer to the idols themselves, which are inanimate and have no knowledge; Ibn Atiyya considers this possible but weak. As for the portion set aside, most exegetes, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify it with the crops and livestock offered to the idols. Al-Hasan links it to the practices of the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham, and al-Razi mentions the belief that some goods came through the help of particular idols. Regarding the questioning, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya understand it as a question meant as rebuke and reproach. Al-Razi holds that it will take place on the Last Day, while others place it at the approach of death or in the grave. The commentators draw no specific legal ruling here; the emphasis is on blame and warning against the polytheists.

This verse condemns the folly of the idolaters who attributed daughters to God, although He is exalted above having offspring, while they reserved for themselves the sons they desired. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the tribes of Khuza'a and Kinana claimed the angels were God's daughters, and they explain that the phrase "Glory be to Him" declares God free of this claim. Ibn Kathir adds that the verse also condemns the injustice of their division. The commentators agree that these people were ashamed at the birth of a daughter: the face darkened and the father hid himself from his people. Al-Mawardi records three readings of "darkened": a true dark colour according to the majority, a change of complexion according to Muqatil, and grief according to al-Zajjaj. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that "kazim" means one who swallows his grief. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur note that "zalla" can mean "became" or "remained". The word "hawn" is read as humiliation by al-Yazidi and Ibn Kathir, and as scarcity by al-Farra'. The word "dass" means burying, that is, burying the girl alive. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi describe the forms this infanticide took and cite related reports. All the commentators agree that the verse ends by condemning their judgement. The disagreements concern mainly the grammar of "ma" and certain vocabulary meanings.

This verse describes the pagans who attributed daughters to God while rejecting them for themselves: when one of them was given the news of a daughter, his face darkened and he was filled with grief and suppressed anger. The commentators explain that kazim means one who is full of sorrow or who swallows his anger without showing it. According to them, he hid from his people out of shame at the news, then wavered between keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her alive in the earth, and God rebukes this judgment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that this was the custom of the pre-Islamic Arabs, and al-Razi adds that several tribes, including Khuza'a, Kinana, Mudar and Tamim, practised it. On the meaning of the darkened face, al-Mawardi lists three views: literal blackness, which he says the majority held, a change of colour reported from Muqatil, and a figurative image of grief, preferred by al-Zajjaj and others. Ibn 'Ashur explains it as an expression of humiliation and shame. Regarding the phrase the highest similitude, most commentators take it as God's perfection and unity, Ibn Sa'di links it to all the attributes of perfection, and Qatada to the testimony of faith.

This verse describes the reaction of some Arabs in the pre-Islamic period when a daughter was born: the man hides from his people out of shame at the news, then wavers between keeping the child in humiliation or burying her alive. The commentators explain that hun means disgrace and that dassa means to bury. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that infanticide was practised among Mudar, Khuza'a and Tamim, out of fear of poverty or the greed of unworthy suitors. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi read the darkened face as a figure for grief and sorrow, whereas al-Mawardi reports that most scholars take it as a literal change of colour, while preferring the sense of sadness. On who is humiliated in the phrase about keeping her in humiliation, Ibn 'Abbas holds that it is the father who keeps the child despite his own abasement, while others take it to refer to the girl. Al-Razi notes that the aversion to daughters reached the point of killing, and he uses this to argue against attributing offspring to God. The scholars agree that the verse rebukes the polytheists who assign daughters to God while rejecting them for themselves. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the highest similitude belongs to God as perfection and monotheism, while the evil similitude, according to Ibn 'Abbas, is the Fire. Several commentators stress that the verdict the people pass is dreadful, and Abu al-Su'ud explains it as an inversion of what is fitting.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the account of the pagan Arabs who attributed daughters to God while disliking them for themselves. The phrase "mathal al-saw'" refers to the base, deficient quality of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, while "al-mathal al-a'la" refers to the supreme quality that belongs to God and is free of any defect. The scholars differ on the details. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada and Mujahid, understands the supreme quality as monotheism and the testimony that there is no god but God, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as God's absolute perfection and freedom from any resemblance to creatures. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain the evil as the need for sons, the aversion to daughters and their burial for fear of poverty, and the good as God's independence from all beings and His generosity. Ibn Atiyya rejects reading "mathal" as merely "sifa" and keeps its literal sense, since saying the daughters belong to God is itself a comparison attributed to Him. Al-Razi lists several possibilities, including ignorance and disbelief, or the attribution of spouse and offspring to God. Al-Qurtubi also reports that some took the evil similitude to mean punishment and the Fire. Al-Tabari describes the supreme quality as the most excellent, beautiful and fine. The commentators generally agree that God is the Mighty, whose decree cannot be thwarted, and the Wise, who places everything in its proper place.

This verse says that if God punished people immediately for their wrongdoing, meaning their disbelief and sins, He would leave no creature crawling on the earth. In His forbearance, however, He delays them until a fixed term, and when that term arrives they cannot delay it by a moment or hasten it. Commentators disagree on the scope of the punishment and of the word people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand a general destruction that also reaches animals, citing reports from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra that the beetle and the bustard perish because of the sins of the children of Adam. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note a narrower reading, limiting the verse to wrongdoers, while al-Jubba'i keeps the word creature in its general sense. As for the fixed term, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Day of Resurrection, whereas al-Baydawi and al-Razi also mention the end of each person's life or the continuation of the species. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument about the infallibility of the prophets, which al-Alusi discusses by distinguishing levels of fault. The passage then turns to those who attribute to God the daughters they dislike and claim the best reward for themselves; the commentators see this as a rebuttal announcing the Fire. They also differ on the reading of the word mufrafun: Nafi' reads it with a kasra and a light shadda-less form meaning those who exceed the limits, most readers take it as those hastened into the Fire or left forgotten there, and Abu Ja'far reads it with a shadda meaning those who neglect their duty.

This verse describes the idolaters who attribute to God what they dislike for themselves, which most commentators take to be daughters, and which some extend to partners in authority, contempt for the messengers, and inferior wealth. Their tongues utter the lie that they will have the best reward with God, and God replies that they will surely have the Fire and be left behind in it. Most commentators understand al-husna as sons, as Mujahid and Qatada report, namely the Quraysh saying that they have the sons while God has the daughters. Al-Zajjaj takes it to mean a good reward from God, while al-Tabari links it to the Day of Resurrection. Some say they spoke this on the supposition that resurrection is true. On the meaning of mufrattun, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn Abbas say forgotten and left behind in the Fire, while Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Farra' say hastened ahead of others toward it, like the forerunner who goes ahead to the water. Nafi's reading with a kasra, mufrifun, means those who exceed the bounds in sins, and Abu Ja'far's reading mufarrifun means those who neglect what is owed. Al-Tabari prefers the common reading and its meaning of abandoned and forgotten, which he considers most correct.

This verse swears by God that He sent messengers to earlier nations, and that Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, so that he became their patron in this world, and a painful punishment awaits them. Most commentators read it as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ facing the rejection of his people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the word 'patron' as a helper or companion in this life, and Ibn Kathir adds that on the Day of Judgment they will be under punishment while Satan cannot free them. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take 'today' as the time of the narration, the span of worldly life, or the Day of Resurrection, and treat the phrasing as a vivid narration of a past or future scene. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the phrase can refer to the lifetime of those peoples. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi suggest the pronoun may refer to the Quraysh, who are of the same kind as those nations, or that a noun such as 'the likes of them' is implied. Al-Razi reports the Mu'tazilite argument from this verse that human acts are created by humans, and answers that the one who embellishes the evil must ultimately be God. The commentators link the verse to the next, which states that the Quran was revealed to clarify the matters in dispute and as guidance and mercy for believers.

This verse states that God sent down the Qur'an to His Messenger so that he might make clear to people what they differ about in religion and rulings, and that it is a guidance and mercy for those who believe. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree that the Book decides between people in their disputes, that the clarifying belongs to the Prophet in conveying and explaining it, while guidance and mercy are actions of the One who sent the Book down; for this reason the two words are in the accusative, in coordination with the position of the particle of purpose. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi specify that the disagreement covers monotheism, polytheism, resurrection, predestination and what is lawful and unlawful, and al-Nasafi singles out resurrection, since some in his people believed in it. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy note that mentioning the believers reflects that they are the ones who benefit from the Qur'an, while al-Razi holds that it is also guidance for others. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir read the passage as a consolation to the Prophet over his people's rejection. Ibn 'Atiyya links the guidance to the argument from rain, offered as a sign of divine lordship. The commentators agree on the general meaning; they differ over the kind of disagreement intended and over whether guidance and mercy apply to believers alone or to all people.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls the blessing of rain sent down from the sky, by which God brings the dry earth back to life with vegetation after its barrenness, and that it is a clear sign of God's oneness and power, and of the possibility of resurrection, just as the earth is revived after its death. Most agree that "water" means rain and that the revival of the earth is a figure for plants growing after they had withered, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari. As for "for a people who hear", most read it as hearing with reflection and fairness: whoever does not listen with his heart is like a deaf man, according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi. Al-Tabari takes it as those who hear the statement, reflect on it and obey God, while al-Baghawi specifies that this is the hearing of the hearts, not of the ears. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan connect the verse to what precedes it, seeing it as a blessing and a lesson about lordship, since rain is the clearest of favours and the basis of life. Ibn 'Ashur follows this reading and sees in hearing a way of expressing fairness and compliance, since the proof is plainly visible. The commentators thus agree on the general sense of the verse; their differences concern mainly the precise meaning of hearing and the place of this argument within the surah.

This verse presents the livestock as a sign for people: they are given to drink milk that comes out from between the contents of the stomach and the blood, pure, with neither the colour of blood nor the smell of dung, and easy to swallow. The commentators explain that food in the rumen separates into three parts, with dung at the bottom, milk in the middle and blood at the top; the liver then sends the blood through the veins and the milk to the udder, while the dung stays in the stomach. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the purpose of the sign is to point to God's power, wisdom and kindness. They differ over the pronoun in 'their bellies': al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i refer it to the cattle or to what was mentioned, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i in another report take it to mean the part of the animals that give milk, since males give none. On the reading 'nuskikum', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold the two forms to be dialects with the same meaning, while Abu 'Ubayd prefers the form with a dammah because the drink is constant. Ibn al-'Arabi rejects the claim of al-Naqqash that the verse proves the purity of semen, a point al-Qurtubi discusses at length. Jurists draw from the verse the permissibility of drinking milk and the prohibition of milk from a dead animal, and the verse is read as a reminder to give thanks for this favour.

This verse names one of God's favours: from the fruits of the date palm and the vine, people make an intoxicant and a good provision. The commentators differ widely on the meaning of "sakar". Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and others take it to mean wine, and hold that the verse was revealed before wine was forbidden and was later abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'ida. A different report from Ibn Abbas, also transmitted by al-Awfi, says sakar is vinegar in the Abyssinian language. Abu Ubayda takes it to mean food, and al-Tabari prefers this reading, since it leaves the verse unabrogated. The Hanafis, including Abu Hanifa, understand sakar as non-intoxicating fermented drinks, arguing that God only praises what is lawful, while the majority reply with the hadiths forbidding every intoxicant. Al-Sha'bi, in another report, identifies it with nabidh. As for the "good provision", most identify it with dates, raisins, vinegar, grape syrup and similar foods. The verse concludes that these are signs for people who use their reason, which the commentators note is the noblest faculty of the human being.

The commentators explain that God inspired the bees, or placed in their hearts, to build their dwellings in the mountains, in trees, and in the structures people make for them, then to feed on all kinds of fruits and flowers and to follow the paths their Lord has made easy for them, so that a drink of varied colours, honey, comes out of their bellies. Most of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, agree that the revelation means inspiration and the subjection of the bee to a natural guidance. They read the particle "min" as partitive, since bees do not build in every mountain or tree. The majority hold that the pronoun in "wherein is healing for mankind" refers to the honey, citing the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about the man whose brother had a stomach complaint; Mujahid takes it to mean the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir considers the first view the sounder one. On "ya'rishun", Ibn Zayd understands vineyards, al-Tabari roofs that are built, and others a wider meaning. On the paths described as "dhulul", Mujahid says they are not rugged for the bees, Qatada says the bees themselves are obedient, and some combine both readings. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim describe at length the marvels of the hexagonal cells and the organisation of the hive, while others only allude to them. The overall lesson is a sign of God's knowledge, power and wisdom for those who reflect.

This verse describes how God inspires the bee to build its hives in mountains, trees and structures people raise, then to feed on all kinds of fruit and return to its hive along paths made easy for it. From its body comes a drink of varied colours, honey, which contains healing for people. The commentators agree that this is a great sign of God's power and wisdom, and that the verse calls for reflection. They differ on the meaning of the inspiration: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as guidance, while al-Hasan takes it as instincts placed in the bee's nature. On the word "dhululan", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy link it to the paths, which are made smooth, whereas Qatada and Ibn Zayd link it to the bee, which is obedient and submissive. On the pronoun in "fihi", most, including Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, refer it to honey, while Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' refer it to the Qur'an; al-Tabari prefers honey as fitting the context. As for the extent of the cure, Ibn Mas'ud says honey cures every illness, but al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the text does not imply universality and that honey works in some cases. The hadith of the brother with a stomach ailment, reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim, is cited by most as evidence of its benefit. All conclude that the verse invites reflection on creation.

This verse says that God creates people, then takes them at the end of their terms, and that some are returned to the lowest point of life, the decrepit age in which a person becomes weak again as in childhood and loses what he once knew. The commentators agree on the general meaning of this age of decline but differ on its length. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report from Ali that it is seventy-five years, while Qatada places it at ninety and Qutrub at eighty. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi hold that it varies from person to person and is not bound to a fixed number, and al-Razi explains it as the natural weakening of the vital powers. On the phrase 'so that he knows nothing after knowing', al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as a forgetfulness like that of childhood, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as a sign of diminished knowledge rather than total ignorance. Al-Mawardi offers that it may refer to the cessation of action after knowledge. The verse ends by affirming God's perfect knowledge and power. For the following verse on unequal provision, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada see a parable against idolaters: masters would not share their wealth equally with their slaves, so how can they make servants into partners of God? Ibn 'Abbas also links it to the Christians of Najran. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya transmit these views, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that denial presupposes prior knowledge.

In this verse God states that He has favoured some people over others in provision: some are rich and some poor, some are masters and some slaves. The meaning most commentators adopt, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, is that masters do not give their slaves a share of their wealth so as to become equal to them. If they refuse such equality for themselves, how can they make creatures partners of God? On this reading the verse refutes the polytheists who worshipped idols alongside God, and the word translated as ingratitude means denying God's blessing. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, also links the passage to the Christians of Najran who said Jesus was the son of God, while Qatada sees it as a parable about one who shares his wife and bed with a slave and then equates God with others.

Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi offer another reading: God provides for both masters and slaves, and the master merely passes on what God has given him. Al-Zamakhshari links this reading to a call to treat slaves kindly, citing a report from Abu Dharr. Ibn Juzayy considers the first meaning the stronger one. Al-Razi sets out both views and explains several ways in which polytheism amounts to ingratitude.

On recitation, Abu Bakr, transmitting from 'Asim, reads the verb in the second person, while the majority read it in the third person, which Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer because the subject is closer.

This verse recounts God's favours upon people: He created for them spouses of their own kind with whom they find rest and affection, gave them children and grandchildren through them, and provided them with good things, and then rebukes them for believing in falsehood and denying God's blessing. The commentators agree on this general sense. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the spouses are of the same kind as the men, which produces harmony and affection. The meaning of 'hafada' is where scholars differ. Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i and Abu al-Duha take them to be in-laws, the sons-in-law and relatives of the wife. Ibn Abbas in one report, and Ibn Kathir, take them to be grandchildren or the children of a wife by another husband. Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Hasan and Tawus take them to be servants and helpers. Al-Tabari holds that all these senses fall within the meaning of prompt service and that none should be excluded, whereas al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi regard grandchildren as the most apparent sense. On the good things, most cite fruits, grains and food; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that 'min' is partitive, since complete goods belong to Paradise. On the 'falsehood', Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say it means idols, Muqatil says Satan, and others say it means what the polytheists forbade, such as the bahira and sa'iba. Denying the blessing, the commentators explain, means ascribing the favours to idols or forbidding what God has made lawful.

God states that those who worship besides Him idols that possess no provision for them, neither rain from the heavens nor produce from the earth, and are utterly unable to do so. The commentators read the verse as a demonstration of the powerlessness of the objects of worship and a rebuke to their worshippers, since whoever cannot provide sustenance is unfit to be worshipped. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir agree that the idols cannot send rain or make plants grow, and that the plural pronoun in 'nor are they able' refers to the idols, following the belief of their worshippers. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya note that it may instead refer to the disbelievers themselves, who, though living and active, cannot do this, let alone lifeless things. The phrase 'do not coin similitudes for God' is taken by most to forbid likening God to His creation or assigning Him rivals, and al-Tabari adds that God knows the right and wrong of such comparisons while people do not. Grammarians differ on the role of 'a thing': al-Akhfash takes it as an apposition to 'provision', while al-Farra and the Kufans take it as the object of the verbal noun 'provision', a view Ibn Atiyya considers stronger and al-Zamakhshari allows as well. Most exegetes identify the heavenly provision as rain and the earthly provision as plants. A few commentaries also read the surrounding parable of a slave unable to do anything against a free man with generous means, but most apply it to God and the idols.

This verse forbids attributing equals, likenesses or rivals to God. It comes after a list of divine favours and after the point that the idols own no provision from heaven or earth and cannot act. The commentators explain that "striking similitudes" means associating God with something else: whoever draws a comparison likens one situation or one thing to another. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take the "similitudes" to mean equals or counterparts, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Razi stress that God is one and has no like. On the closing phrase, "God knows and you do not know," the scholars differ. Muqatil and Ibn al-Sa'ib take it to mean that God knows He has no partner, which people fail to see. Others, such as al-Tabari, read it as a warning that God knows the consequences of what they do. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi regard the phrase as the reason for the prohibition: God knows the gravity of the act, and ignorance is what led people to commit it. Al-Razi offers a further reading: the idolaters reasoned by analogy with kings, saying that the stars and idols are servants of the supreme God, and the text orders them to drop this analogy because revealed text takes precedence over reasoning. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the verse is followed by the parable of the slave and the master, which the commentators apply either to the disbeliever and the believer or to God against the idols.

In this verse God offers two examples: a slave, wholly under his master's control, who owns nothing and can do nothing, and a free man whom God has granted lawful provision, and who spends from it openly and in secret. He then asks whether the two are equal, the obvious answer being no, and concludes with 'Praise be to God; but most of them do not know.' The commentators agree that the purpose of the parable is to refute polytheism, since the Creator, who is master and powerful, cannot be placed on the same level as idols that have no power. Regarding the identity of the two figures, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read them as images of the disbeliever, a slave to his desires who cannot benefit from his deeds, and of the believer, who spends in obedience to God. Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Baghawi, by contrast, take it as a parable of God Himself set against the idols, which are the powerless slave. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi discuss from this verse whether a slave can legally own property, and al-Qurtubi reports the positions of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the Iraqi school without deciding between them. Some reports link the verse to particular people, such as Uthman or Abu Jahl, but Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider these chains unsound. On the word 'most', al-Razi and others take it as general, while others understand it as leaving room for those who know and still reject the truth.

This verse presents a second parable of two men: one is mute and deaf, unable to understand or be understood, incapable of doing anything, and a burden on whoever looks after him, failing in every errand he is sent on. The other speaks, has ability, commands justice and walks a straight path. The commentators agree that the comparison highlights the gap between the idol, which neither benefits nor harms, and God, who commands justice and guides to the straight path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada, followed by Mujahid, apply it to God and the idol: the mute man is the idol, which must be carried and served, and the one who commands justice is God. Ibn Abbas, by contrast, reads it as the unbeliever and the believer, the mute being the unbeliever and the one who commands justice the believer, and another report links it to Uthman ibn Affan and a freed slave who refused Islam. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur take the passage as a second example contrasting God's attributes with those of idols, without naming particular people. Al-Razi holds that the most fitting reading covers any person who has these blameworthy traits and any person who has these praiseworthy ones, and he does not prefer one exegesis over the others. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir stress the clearer meaning, which condemns polytheism and affirms God's justice. Several commentators note that the variety of interpretations does not change the central point of the comparison, namely that the helpless cannot be equal to the Mighty and the Wise.

This verse affirms that knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, and that the coming of the Hour will be as quick as a glance of the eye, or quicker still, since when God wills something He says "Be" and it is. Commentators agree on this general meaning and on the context: the verse answers the Quraysh who asked about the Hour or mocked it, as al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, and it belongs to a passage on God's oneness and the completeness of His knowledge and power. They differ on the meaning of "the unseen": al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to be the Hour itself, while al-Tabari and most exegetes take it as whatever is hidden from creatures, and al-Mawardi offers five readings, including the bringing into being of what does not exist and the annihilation of what exists.

The phrase "or it is nearer" has been read in several ways. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the particle to express doubt as seen from the listener's side, or a choice in some views. Al-Farra' understands it as meaning "rather," and al-Baydawi and al-Alusi likewise read it as moving to a stronger term. Al-Zajjaj sees a deliberate vagueness for the audience, and al-Razi holds that it points to something even quicker. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as an image of nearness, ease and speed. Ibn Sa'di stresses that once the Hour arrives it will take no longer than the blink of an eye.

The verse ends by affirming God's absolute power, and several commentators draw from it the possibility of resurrection. The following verses recall that God brings humans out of their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, and gives them hearing, sight and hearts so that they may give thanks.

This verse recalls God's favour in bringing people out of their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then giving them hearing, sight and hearts so that they may gain knowledge and be thankful to their Lord. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read the phrase 'knowing nothing' as a circumstantial clause attached to the subject of 'brought forth', meaning that you were born ignorant of everything, and that God then gave you the means of knowledge. Most commentators understand hearing, sight and hearts as instruments of perception: hearing for sounds, sight for visible things, and the hearts, meaning the intellects, for understanding and discernment. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi also see in them the capacity to perceive God's signs and admonitions.

The commentators agree that the verse belongs to the proofs of God's oneness and that gratitude is the purpose of these gifts. Knowledge begins with the senses and then reaches the intellect. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the devoted servant whose hearing and sight God becomes, showing that the limbs are to be used in obedience.

On linguistic matters, the readers differ on the vowels of 'ummahatikum', and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the letter ha is an added element. On the meaning of 'knowing nothing', opinions differ: some take it to refer to the covenant taken in the loins of the fathers, others to the decree of happiness or misery, and others to one's benefits, though many prefer the general sense. Ibn al-Qayyim describes stages of knowledge from touch up to prophecy. Al-Razi links the acquisition of necessary knowledge to the senses, while Ibn 'Ashur explains the grammatical forms used for hearing, sight and hearts.

This verse draws attention to birds flying in subjection in the air between heaven and earth, and to the fact that none but God holds them up. The commentators explain that subjection means that God has made them able to fly, through the wings and favourable means He gave them, and that flight is not in their nature alone. Most, such as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, agree that the holding up refers to the folding and spreading of the wings, and that the weight of their bodies would bring them down without God's power. They read in this signs that point to God's oneness and to the falsehood of worshipping idols, and they note that these signs benefit only believers, who are the ones who draw a lesson from them. Al-Tabari adds that the believers are those who accept what their eyes see and their senses perceive. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan go into the design of the bird, the lightness of its body and the shape of its wings. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi mention only the wings and suitable means of flight. The readers differ between ya and ta in the verb 'have they not seen', without changing the meaning. Al-Razi attributes the holding up to God, since He gives the instruments of flight, and he answers the Mu'tazili objection that human acts are created by God. Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn say only that God holds them when they fold or spread their wings.

This verse lists God's blessings concerning dwellings. The commentators agree on the general meaning: God made your houses of stone and clay a place of residence and rest, and made tents and pavilions from the hides of livestock that are light to carry when travelling and easy to pitch when staying. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the wool comes from sheep, the hair of camels from camels, and the goat hair from goats, and that athath means household goods such as rugs and coverings. Ibn Abbas understands it as wealth, while Mujahid understands it as belongings. The phrase matta' ila hin is explained by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid as until death, and by Muqatil as until the object wears out and perishes. Scholars differ on whether tents made of wool and hair fall under the phrase 'hides of livestock'. Ibn Salam includes them, since such materials grow on the hide, and al-Baydawi allows this as a possibility, while others hold that the primary sense is tents of leather. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that cotton and linen are not mentioned because they were not found in the land of the Arabs addressed, though the word sarabil covers them. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite Ata al-Khurasani, who said the Quran speaks in terms of the knowledge of its listeners, which explains the mention of mountains and heat. Readers differ on the vowelling of the word for travel, both forms being accepted by most commentators. Few commentators rely on a specific occasion of revelation, although Ibn Kathir reports an account of a Bedouin who affirmed each blessing before turning away.

This passage recalls a blessing of God toward people: He gave them shade to shelter from the sun's heat, caves and hollows in the mountains to dwell in, garments that protect from heat, and coats of mail that protect them from the violence of war. The commentators agree that the shade refers to whatever casts shade, such as trees, buildings or mountains, that the akman are caves and grottoes, and that the sarabil are shirts of cotton, linen or wool, as well as armour that guards against harm, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report. On why heat is named without cold, opinions differ. Ata al-Khurasani, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, holds that the Quran addressed the Arabs in terms of their own experience, since their land was hot and mountainous; al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj hold that naming one opposite suffices to imply the other, citing the well-known verse; al-Zamakhshari and al-Qasimi argue that protection from heat was more important to them. Ibn Abbas's reading tasalamun, meaning safety from wounds, is explained by most, while Abu 'Ubayd prefers the common reading tuslimun, meaning faith and submission.

On the phrase they recognise God's blessing and then deny it, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir take the blessings listed as the referent, whose divine source they deny by attributing them to their forefathers or their idols, while al-Suddi, al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the Prophet ﷺ to be meant. Al-Hasan holds that 'most of them' means all of them, and al-Mawardi and al-Razi explain that the phrase excludes those who are not accountable.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that if the idolaters turn away from his call and reject it, he bears no blame and no shortcoming, because his duty is only to deliver the message clearly, and he has done so. The commentators link the verse to the list of divine blessings just before it, including homes, shade, mountains, garments and armour, which God completes so that people might submit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the Quraysh acknowledge these favours as coming from God and then deny them by worshipping others, by claiming they inherited them from their fathers, or by attributing them to the intercession of their idols. Al-Suddi, followed by al-Tabari, takes "the favour" to be the Prophet himself, whom they recognise and then call a liar; al-Tabari prefers this reading because it fits the surrounding verses. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that "thumma" (then) signals that denial after recognition is startling. Al-Hasan holds that "most of them" means all of them, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the word may exclude children or those who never received the proof. Ibn 'Atiyya mentions that some regard the verse as abrogated by the verse of the sword, though this view is not shared by all. The common ground is that guidance does not rest with the Prophet, whose task is only to convey the message.

The verse says that if the idolaters turn away, the Prophet ﷺ bears no blame, since he has delivered the clear message. It then describes them as recognising God's favour and yet denying it. The commentators differ on what this favour is. As-Suddi, followed by at-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understood it as the Prophet's mission, so that denying it meant calling him a liar; at-Tabari preferred this reading because the verse sits between two passages about the Messenger and his mission. Mujahid and Qatada took it to mean the blessings listed in the surah: they admit these come from God but claim to have inherited them from their fathers. Al-Kalbi reports that they attributed these gifts to the intercession of their idols, and Awn ibn Abd Allah gives the example of someone saying that without a certain person he would not have obtained something. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi regard such attitudes as forms of ingratitude.

Most exegetes agree that the favour covers all the blessings enumerated in the surah, and that the denial lies in worshipping other than the Giver, as Ibn al-Qayyim explains. Az-Zamakhshari and ar-Razi explain the word "then" as signalling that denial after recognition is a surprising thing.

On the phrase "and most of them are disbelievers", al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and as-Sam'ani understood that all of them are meant, the word "most" standing for the whole. Ar-Razi and al-Baydawi offer other explanations: some lacked the capacity to discern or had not reached the age of responsibility, or the majority may stand for the whole.

This verse says that on the Day of Resurrection God will raise from every community a witness, its prophet, who will testify for those who believed and against those who disbelieved, according to what he conveyed to them. The disbelievers will then not be permitted to offer excuses, and they will not be asked to satisfy their Lord, because the Hereafter is not a place of obligation and they will not be sent back to the world to repent. The commentators agree that the permission being denied is permission to make excuses, and that the word istiʿtab means seeking to have one's blame removed and one's Lord's displeasure lifted, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi report. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the particle thumma indicates that being denied the right to excuse is a greater affliction than the testimony of the prophets, a view echoed by al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani.

Al-Tabari, however, understands the phrase about not being satisfied to mean that they are not granted a return to the world to repent, a reading that Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan find plausible. Others take it simply to mean that they are not asked to please God, as Ibn al-Qayyim argues while distinguishing the Lord's displeasure from the servant's seeking of pardon.

The following part, describing the punishment that will not be lightened and the associators facing their idols, was discussed by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who mention scorpions, serpents and rivers of molten brass. Ibn Kathir adopts these descriptions, while al-Tabari prefers a different reading. Ibn 'Ashur notes that being denied permission may also mean outright rejection.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of the wrongdoers, those who disbelieved and associated partners with God. When they see the punishment, meaning Hell, it will not be lightened for them and they will not be given respite, because the time for repentance has passed and the Hereafter is a place of recompense, not of action. The verse belongs to the description of the Day of Resurrection, in which God raises from every nation a witness, its prophet, and the disbelievers are not permitted to offer excuses nor asked to seek to please their Lord.

Most exegetes agree on the general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that the punishment never slackens and that no delay is granted, while al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud clarify that the respite refers to being postponed before the punishment. Ibn Juzayy and al-Shawkani connect the verse with the passage in Surah al-Anbiya' where the punishment seizes the disbelievers suddenly. The Jalalayn and al-Jaza'iri read it as a warning and a reminder, and Sayyid Qutb links it to the moment when the false gods turn away from their worshippers.

The main disagreement concerns grammar. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi report that the unmarked future verb suggests the clause is the answer of the conditional, whereas al-Zamakhshari holds that the answer is implied and that the fa' is explanatory. Al-Razi draws from the absence of relief the idea that the punishment is free of any benefit, and from the absence of respite that it is eternal; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi consider this reasoning open to question. Ibn 'Ashur finally observes that the aim of the verse is to express the severity of the torment, from which one cannot hope to escape as one might hope to escape the calamities of this world.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Judgement, when those who associated partners with God see the beings they worshipped besides Him and say: Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You. Those partners answer them with a denial: indeed, you are liars. The commentators explain this denial in closely related ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that the idols deny that they were gods, since they were inanimate objects that did not know who worshipped them. Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud report that the denial may concern the claim of being worshipped, or that the worship was not true worship because those worshipped did not approve of it, as Zamakhshari also notes. As for demons, they may be lying about their claim to divinity, while God makes the idols speak at that moment. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi offer two possible purposes for the associators' words: to shift blame onto their idols in hope of relief, or to acknowledge their error. The commentators agree that the associators then submit to God and His judgement, and that what they had invented, the intercession of their gods, vanishes. Regarding the increase of punishment, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr describe it in vivid images such as scorpions, serpents and rivers of molten brass, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi relate it to those who disbelieved and barred others from God's path. Each community's witness is, according to them, its own prophet.

The commentators explain that on the Day of Resurrection the polytheists will submit to God and humble themselves before His judgment, after having been arrogant in this world, and that what they fabricated, namely that their deities would intercede for them or help them, will vanish and be lost to them. The exegetes agree that the phrase "alqaw ilaa Allah as-salam" means surrender and submission, and that "dalla" means to go astray in the sense of being lost or failing. Al-Tabari understands it as the abandonment of the idolaters by their gods, their peoples and clans who had defended them in this world. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: submission to God's punishment, or acknowledgement of what they had denied regarding obedience to Him. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi hold that the worshipper and the worshipped both submit together. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy link the submission to the end of their former arrogance. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud keep close to this general sense, adding that the false belief in intercession collapses. As for the meaning of going astray, al-Razi mentions two senses: the disappearance of the belief in intercession, or the disappearance of what Satan had made attractive, namely associating partners with God and claiming He had a son. On the recitation, Ibn 'Atiyya reports that most readers pronounce "as-salam" with a fatha, that Ya'qub reads it with a sukun, and that Mujahid reads "as-sulam".

This verse states that those who disbelieved and barred others from the path of God will receive a punishment added to the punishment they already deserve, because of the corruption they spread. The commentators describe this added punishment in several ways. Ibn Mas'ud, reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, speaks of scorpions with fangs like tall palm trees and serpents with long necks. Ibn 'Abbas, cited by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, speaks of five rivers of molten brass flowing from beneath the Throne, by which the damned are tormented three times at night and twice by day. Al-Zajjaj, quoted by al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, describes them passing from the heat of the Fire to the bitter cold of zamharir, and then rushing back to the Fire.

The commentators agree that the added punishment is due to two sins: disbelief in oneself and leading others into disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud state this clearly. Ibn al-Qayyim cites the verse in al-'Ankabut about bearing one's own burdens and those of the people one misled, along with the hadith on whoever starts an evil practice. Ibn Kathir notes that the disbelievers differ in their punishment just as believers differ in their ranks. Al-Razi argues that calling others to error is graver than disbelief alone. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the word for punishment is definite in the first case and indefinite in the second, since the second is less familiar. Al-Alusi reports that some take the added punishment as greater severity, others as a result of persisting in the sin. Al-Shawkani and al-Jaza'iri keep close to the text and stress the warning against leading others astray.

This verse says that on the Day of Resurrection God will raise up in every community a witness from among its own people, namely its prophet, and that Muhammad ﷺ will be a witness over his own community. The commentators also explain that the Qur'an was sent down as an explanation of everything people need, the lawful and the unlawful, reward and punishment, a guidance away from error, a mercy and a glad tiding for the Muslims. They agree that the witness is the prophet, sent from among the people themselves.

On the meaning of "tibyan li-kulli shay'", opinions differ in emphasis. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid stress what is lawful and unlawful, or what is commanded and forbidden, while Ibn Mas'ud states that every useful knowledge is set out in the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan hold that the Book explains the matters of religion, either directly or by referring to the Sunna, consensus and analogy, because all of these go back to the Book, which commands obedience to the Prophet. Al-Razi reports broader views, holding that the principles of belief are fully set out, while the legal details also rest on consensus and analogy. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi add that the verse is also taken as a confirmation that the Qur'an leaves no excuse.

On the meaning of "shahid", al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi say the witnesses are the prophets, or, in another view, the scholars and guides who preserve the prophetic law. Al-Razi and al-Alusi report the opinion of al-Asamm that the witnesses are the parts of the human body that speak on that day, but most commentators reject it as not fitting the context. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the Prophet's testimony over his community, while Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as closing off any excuse for those who refuse.

This comprehensive verse sets out the core principles of conduct. God commands justice, excellence in doing good, and giving to close relatives, and forbids indecency, what is reprehensible, and oppression, so that people may take heed and remember. Commentators give several meanings to justice: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as the testimony that there is no god but God, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna as equality between what is hidden and what is shown in one's deeds, and 'Ali as fairness. For Ibn 'Abbas, excellence (ihsan) means performing the religious duties, while others understand it as sincerity, forgiveness or generosity, and many cite the hadith of Gabriel about worshipping God as if you see Him. All agree that giving to relatives means maintaining family ties and helping them. Indecency (fahsha) is taken by Ibn 'Abbas to mean adultery, though it is generally understood as any grave wrong; what is reprehensible (munkar) is what the law and sound reason reject; and oppression (baghy) means wronging people and arrogance, which several scholars regard as a sin with swift consequences in this life. Ibn Mas'ud called it the most comprehensive verse in the Quran for good and evil, and it is said to have led to the conversion of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim relate the prohibitions to the faculties of the soul, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya distinguish obligatory duties from recommended acts. The purpose of the verse is that the believer remember and be admonished.

In this verse God commands believers to keep their covenants and not to break oaths after confirming them, since they have made God their guarantor and witness. The commentators agree that fidelity is obligatory but differ on what the covenant refers to. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it may be the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ upon embracing Islam, while Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd see it as the alliances of the pre-Islamic era which Islam confirmed. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the wording is general and covers any commitment freely undertaken. Al-Sha'bi and al-Baghawi take the covenant to mean the oath itself, whose expiation is that of an oath, and Ibn 'Abbas and Umar include promises. The word kafil is explained as witness and watcher. The parable of the woman who unravels her thread after spinning it is attributed by al-Kalbi and Muqatil to a specific woman named Rayta of Quraysh, whereas Ibn Kathir and Qatada treat it as a general image. The word dakhal means deceit, and the phrase a community greater than another refers to allying with the stronger group. Al-Tabari notes the trial may concern the advantage of numbers or fidelity itself.

In this verse God forbids believers from breaking their oaths and covenants after they have been confirmed, and illustrates the point with a woman who unravels the thread she has spun and twisted, leaving only useless strands. Commentators agree that the verse condemns betrayal of a pledge, and especially the use of an oath as a means of deception, for the sake of an alliance with a group that is more numerous or more powerful.
