Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that this was a practice of the pre-Islamic period, when a tribe allied itself with another and then broke the pact once it found a larger or stronger one. Al-Tabari, following Ibn 'Abbas, takes the word arba to mean 'more numerous', while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also understand greater wealth or standing.

They differ on the occasion of revelation. Mujahid and Qatada link it to the alliances of the Jahiliyya, while a report cited by Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Qurtubi relates it to the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet upon Islam. Al-Zamakhshari sees in the alliances of Quraysh the danger the verse addresses, since they broke pacts when faced with stronger opponents. As for the woman, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi name her Rayta, a well-known fool of Mecca, while Ibn Kathir and Qatada stress that the image is a general one rather than a specific person. Finally, the closing phrase is taken by some to refer back to the command to keep one's word, and by others to wealth and numbers; all agree that God will make clear on the Day of Resurrection what people disputed.

This verse from Surat An-Nahl teaches that God could have made you one single community, meaning, according to most commentators, one religion, Islam. But He did not will it. He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and you will all be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what you did. The apparent meaning is that religious divergence falls under God's will, and that each person is accountable for his deeds.

The commentators agree that the verse serves as a reminder of accountability on the Day of Judgment, and that the will mentioned concerns guidance and misguidance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand guidance as a grace and misguidance as a just abandonment of those whom God knows will choose disbelief, while al-Razi, al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a will of choice rather than compulsion, God creating misguidance or guidance according to what the servant chooses.

Az-Zamakhshari reads the will as compulsion and forcing, holding that divine wisdom founded the matter on free choice, and al-Razi reports the Mu'tazili objection that coercion would void responsibility. Sunni commentators reply that God creates the act while the human has a real acquisition of it. Ibn 'Ashur sees in this will a general disposition of creation, and warns against thinking that those who go astray are excused.

Other commentators, such as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, note that the question asked on the Last Day is one of rebuke and recompense, not of inquiry. They also stress the duty to keep one's oaths, which divergence in belief does not justify breaking. Ibn 'Atiyya links the passage to the image of the woman who unravels her yarn after spinning it firmly.

This part of the verse forbids believers from using their oaths as a means of deception among themselves, lest a foot slip after it had been firm, so that they taste evil in this world and suffer a great punishment in the next. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain the image: a person who was upright and secure falls into ruin, just as a foot slips after standing firm. Most commentators understand 'dakhal' as deceit, treachery or corruption.

The commentators agree that breaking an oath made for deception harms the one who breaks it, that the 'evil' refers to punishment in this world, and that the 'great punishment' is in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir and Sayyid Qutb add that such a breach makes outsiders lose trust in the religion and turn away from it. Al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain 'barring from God's path' as the breaker making it easier for others to break their covenants or to abandon Islam, so that his act becomes an example others follow.

There is a difference of view about the scope. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi hold that the verse addresses those who pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and that breaking that pledge leads to apostasy. Al-Tabari explicitly rejects Mujahid's view that it concerns people who switched their alliances. Abu Hayyan, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur, by contrast, read the prohibition as general, covering every oath, with the pledge to the Prophet as one case among others. Al-Razi also notes that the singular 'foot' stresses that even one slip is a grave matter.

In this verse God commands believers not to exchange the covenant of God for a small worldly price, for what is with God is better for them, if they have understanding. The commentators explain that everything in this world, however abundant, passes away, while what is with God endures, so God will reward those who were patient with the best of their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the verse primarily addresses those who had pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ, and whom the Quraysh tempted with wealth to make them abandon Islam. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, by contrast, take a broader view that covers any bribe or payment taken to abandon a duty. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also relate an occasion of revelation involving a land dispute between two men, in which one withdrew from swearing an oath. Commentators differ on the phrase "the best of what they did": al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to mean obligatory and voluntary acts rather than permissible ones, while Abu Hayyan understands patience itself to be meant. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the emphatic phrasing "it is good for you" stresses that true good lies only with God.

The verse states that what you have runs out, while what is with God endures, and that God will reward those who were patient with the best of their deeds. Commentators link it to the preceding prohibition against breaking oaths and covenants for a small worldly gain: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy read it as showing that even a large worldly price is small compared with God's reward. Al-Tabari takes patience as perseverance in obedience in both ease and hardship, while Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi relate it mainly to enduring the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of Islam. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the singular and indefinite 'foot' stresses how grave it is for even one foot to slip after it has been firmly planted. Al-Razi draws from the verse the proof that the bliss of Paradise does not end, against Jahm ibn Safwan. On the phrase 'the best of their deeds', Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan record several readings: obligatory and recommended acts, a reward greater than their deeds, or patience itself as the best act. Ibn 'Ashur notes that 'what is with God' means what He has stored up for believers in this world and the next. Readers differ between the 'we' form used by Ibn Kathir and Asim and the 'He' form used by most others.

This verse promises that whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, will be granted a good life by God and rewarded with the best of what they did. Most commentators take these words in their plain sense, with the full reward reserved for the Hereafter, and faith as an indispensable condition, since the deeds of disbelievers are not counted toward reward.

The commentators differ on what the 'good life' means. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' understand it as lawful provision, and al-Dahhak adds worship and joy in obedience. Ali, al-Hasan al-Basri and Wahb ibn Munabbih take it as contentment with what God has apportioned, a view repeated by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Qurtubi, identify it with Paradise, and al-Hasan adds that no life is truly good except in Paradise. Abu Bakr al-Warraq describes it as the sweetness of obedience. Al-Mawardi lists further meanings such as happiness, sufficiency and health, or acceptance of the divine decree. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim relate it to the life of the heart through faith and knowledge of God, and al-Razi also reports the view of al-Suddi that it refers to life in the grave. Ibn Kathir concludes that these meanings can all be included, while al-Tabari, after reviewing the reports, ultimately favours contentment.

As for the reward in the best of deeds, al-Mawardi offers two readings: that people are repaid for their best acts, meaning obligatory and recommended ones rather than permissible ones, or that the reward is multiplied. One reported occasion of revelation, transmitted by Abu Salih and cited by al-Tabari, is that people of the Torah, the Gospel and idol worship boasted about their religions.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ, and every reader of the Qur'an after him, to seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan when they intend to recite. The commentators agree that the seeking of refuge comes before the recitation, not after, and that the verse means: when you intend to recite, seek refuge, as one says, when you eat, say the name of God. The majority, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, regard the command as recommended rather than obligatory, while Ata holds it to be obligatory. Abu Hurayra, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, Malik and the reader Hamza, taking the literal sense of the particle fa, hold that it is said after reciting. The most common wording is

This verse states that Satan has no authority over the believers who put their trust in their Lord, and that his power reaches only those who take him as a guardian and obey him. Commentators differ on the meaning of "authority". Most, including Mujahid, al-Nahhas and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean proof, so that Satan has no valid argument for the sins he calls people to. Sufyan al-Thawri understands it as the ability to lead believers into a sin that will not be forgiven, while others hold that he has no power over them at all, citing God's words about Iblis that He excepts His sincere servants. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see seeking refuge in God during recitation as a means of keeping Satan from prevailing, and they cite the verse "if an evil prompting from Satan touches you, seek refuge in God". On the phrase "those who associate partners with Him", Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it as associating others with God, whereas al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Qutayba understand it as associating Satan in their works or acting because of him. Al-Tabari prefers Mujahid's view, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the pronoun may refer either to God or to Satan. On recitation, Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the particle "fa" links the two statements and that "when you recite" means "when you intend to recite". Most scholars regard seeking refuge as recommended, while 'Ata' considered it obligatory. Most jurists place it before the recitation, whereas Abu Hurayra, Dawud and Malik, in one report, placed it after. For most commentators, the Satan meant is Iblis and his helpers.

This verse teaches that seeking refuge in God from the accursed Satan is recommended when reciting the Quran, that Satan has no authority over believers who place their trust in their Lord, and that his authority extends only over those who take him as a protector and obey him. The commentators differed on the meaning of "sultan": Sufyan al-Thawri understood it as the power to lead believers into a sin that is not forgiven, while Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas understood it as proof or dominion. Others held that believers are protected by seeking refuge in God, or that God removed Satan's power from His sincere servants, as Iblis himself says in Surat al-Hijr. The phrase "yatawallawnahu" is taken by most to mean obeying him and taking him as an ally.

The exegetes agree that the seeking of refuge comes before the recitation. Most jurists hold it to be recommended, while 'Ata' considered it obligatory. Abu Hurayra, Malik and Dawud, relying on the literal wording, placed it after the recitation, a view Ibn Kathir and others reject.

They also differed over the phrase "and those who are, because of him, associators". Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari took the pronoun to refer to God, meaning that they associate others with Him, whereas al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Ibn Qutayba and most commentators took it to refer to Satan, with the preposition expressing cause: they associated him with God in their deeds, or became associators because of him. Al-Tabari preferred Mujahid's view, while other exegetes accepted both readings.

This verse says that when God replaces one verse with another, and He knows best what He sends down, the disbelievers called the Prophet ﷺ a mere fabricator, and God replies that most of them do not know. The commentators generally understand the replacement as abrogation, and agree that rulings may change according to what benefits people at a given time. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain that a verse is lifted and another sent in its place, while Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, as reported by al-Razi, takes it to refer to earlier scriptures, such as the change of qibla; al-Razi and others reply that abrogation does occur in this law. The majority, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, hold that abrogation may affect both the wording and the ruling, or the ruling alone. Al-Shafi'i, as cited by al-Razi and al-Shinqiti, held that the Qur'an is abrogated only by the Qur'an, a view others contested. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi note that what is beneficial at one time may become harmful later. The reported occasions of revelation include Quraysh's claim that Muhammad mocks his followers by ordering one thing today and forbidding it tomorrow, and accounts of a foreign slave said to teach the Prophet, which some scholars judge weak. Ibn 'Ashur argues that the replacement covers all variations of aims and contexts, and calls this the best explanation of the verse.

This verse answers the Meccan polytheists who accused the Prophet ﷺ of inventing the Qur'an when they saw a ruling replaced by another. God commands him to tell them that the Qur'an, both its abrogating and abrogated verses, was sent down from his Lord with truth by the Holy Spirit, meaning Gabriel, to make the believers steadfast, and that it is guidance and good news for those who submit. The commentators agree that the Holy Spirit is Gabriel and that qudus means purity. The phrase bi-l-haqq is read as a circumstance: the revelation comes with truth and contains no falsehood. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and most exegetes take tabdil to mean abrogation, whether of the wording and the ruling or of the ruling alone. Al-Razi reports the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, who understood it as changes of the qibla in earlier scriptures, but he notes that most exegetes reject it. Ibn Ashur reads the verse as a reply to the charge of forgery, while Ibn Sa'di stresses that gradual revelation brings greater guidance and good news. Several works, including al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi, mention reports about men said to teach the Prophet, such as Bal'am, Jabr or Yasar, though the latter treats such reports as the accusers' claims rather than established facts. Al-Qasimi argues that the change is itself a sign of the revelation, suited to the Prophet's era.

God reports that the polytheists claimed the Prophet ﷺ did not receive the Qur'an by revelation but was taught it by a human being, and the commentators differ on who this was. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn Juraij name various foreign slaves or youths, such as Balam, Jabr, Ya'ish and Yasar. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that these were Christians who read scripture, while noting that the names differ between transmissions. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud speak of a single man or of two young men without settling their identity. Al-Dahhak names Salman the Persian, a view Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya consider weak, since the surah is Meccan and Salman converted in Medina. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reports a scribe of the revelation who later apostatised, a report Ibn 'Atiyya considers weak. All agree on the divine answer: this man's speech is foreign and unclear, whereas the Qur'an is clear Arabic. The readers differ on the verb yulhidun. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir read it with damma on the first letter, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with fatha; both mean to incline or deviate, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj consider the two meanings close. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur take the clause 'the tongue of the one they incline towards is foreign' as a fresh answer to their claim, though Abu Hayyan also allows it to be a circumstantial clause. Ibn 'Ashur sees the accusation as a pretext invented by the leaders of Quraysh to mislead the common people.

This verse states that those who refuse to believe in the signs of God will not be guided by Him and will suffer a painful punishment. The commentators explain that it responds to the pagans who accused the Prophet ﷺ of inventing the Qur'an. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur present the verse as a rebuttal: it is the disbelievers who fabricate lies, since they neither hope for reward for truthfulness nor fear punishment for lying, whereas the believer dreads lying. On the meaning of the denial of guidance, opinions differ: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as God withholding His favour or the path to Paradise, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di speak of abandonment after people have rejected the truth, and al-Razi lists several readings. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the wording highlights the gravity of their conduct. The following verse on coercion is linked by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who was tortured into uttering words of disbelief while his heart remained firm in faith; he is not blamed, whereas divine wrath falls on whoever opens his breast to disbelief by choice. The jurists, as reported by al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir, agree that uttering a word of disbelief under duress is permitted, but they differ on the divorce of a coerced person: al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad hold that it does not take effect, while Abu Hanifa holds that it does.

This verse states that only those who reject the signs of God invent lies against Him, and that they are the true liars. Commentators such as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that it answers the Meccan polytheists who accused the Prophet ﷺ of being a fabricator, turning the charge back on them. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the phrase "and they are the liars" is an emphasis: lying is a constant trait of theirs, or their lie is the greatest, since rejecting God's signs is the worst falsehood. Ibn Kathir, al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri recall that the Prophet was known for his truthfulness before his mission. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi cite a tradition that a believer does not lie, and al-Sha'rawi draws from it that lying is an especially grave sin.

The following verse, on compulsion, is discussed by al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Most report that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, forced to utter words of disbelief while his heart remained firm in faith, whereas whoever opens his breast to disbelief incurs God's wrath. Ibn Kathir says scholars agree that one under compulsion may speak those words with the tongue, and that enduring death is more meritorious. They differ on whether a divorce pronounced under duress is valid: al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad consider it void, while Abu Hanifa holds it binding.

Commentators also differ on who the Quraysh claimed was teaching the Prophet. Several names are given, and none is settled. They agree, however, on the meaning of "a'jami" as a foreign tongue, set against the clear Arabic of the Qur'an.

This verse distinguishes between the one who disbelieves in God after faith and embraces disbelief willingly, upon whom comes God's wrath and a great punishment, and the one who is forced to utter a word of disbelief while his heart remains firm in faith, who bears no blame. The commentators agree that uttering the word of disbelief is permitted under genuine compulsion. They differ on what is better: most, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, cite the example of Yasir and Sumayya, who were killed rather than renounce, while others hold that taking the concession does not diminish one's merit. According to reports gathered by al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, the verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who was tortured until he said what his tormentors wanted; the Prophet told him that if they returned to force him, he could do the same. On grammar, the Basran and Kufan grammarians disagree on the function of the two occurrences of man, and al-Zajjaj treats the first as an apposition. Jurists debate the validity of a divorce pronounced under duress: al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad consider it void, while Abu Hanifa considers it valid. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi also raise questions about coercion to theft, murder or adultery, on which opinions vary. Several commentators, including al-Razi and al-Baydawi, explain that the punishment is due to preferring the present life to the hereafter, and that God sealed their hearts, hearing and sight, making them utterly heedless and losers in the hereafter.

This verse explains that the wrath of God and the severe punishment promised to the disbelievers fall upon them because they preferred the worldly life and its adornments over the bliss of the Hereafter, and because God does not grant guidance to those who persist in denying His signs. The commentators explain that "that" refers either to the threat or to apostasy after faith, and that "preferred" here means chose and favoured, which does not necessarily imply belief in the Hereafter. They agree that the guidance denied is the guidance of success and steadfastness rather than mere indication of the path; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the verse combines human acquisition of the act with God's creation of disbelief in the heart, in line with Sunni doctrine. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link the following verses to believers who were persecuted, then emigrated and fought. The readings differ: most read "futinu" in the passive, meaning they were tormented or coerced, while Ibn 'Amir reads "fatanu" in the active, meaning they tempted others. Many attribute the revelation to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a or 'Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh; Ibn 'Atiyya considers citing 'Ammar here unsuitable given his rank. On the person forced into disbelief, most allow him to utter a word of unbelief while his heart remains firm in faith, whereas al-Razi considers patience preferable, as the examples of Bilal and Habib ibn Zayd show. All agree that whoever opens his chest to disbelief incurs God's anger and a great punishment.

This verse states that those who abandon faith after knowing it and choose disbelief will incur God's wrath and a great punishment, because they preferred the life of this world to the hereafter. The commentators explain that God sealing their hearts, hearing and sight means their hearts do not grasp the truth, their ears do not benefit from admonition and their eyes do not learn from the signs, and that 'the heedless' are those utterly unaware of what awaits them, since no heedlessness is greater than neglecting the consequences. However, opinions differ on the nature of the sealing: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a seal blocking faith from entering, al-Razi as a mark God creates on the heart, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi describe it as God turning people away from guidance alongside their own chosen aversion. Regarding the exception in the preceding verse, most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, apply it to a person forced to utter a word of disbelief while his heart remains firm in faith, who bears no blame; they report that Ammar ibn Yasir is among those concerned. Others, such as al-Baghawi and al-Razi, also mention 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a or Ibn Abi Sarh. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani extend the concession to coercion in actions, whereas some limit it to speech. The commentators report these views without judging between them.

This passage declares that the real loss will be in the Hereafter for those who disbelieved after faith and preferred the life of this world. The commentators explain that « la jaram » means « undoubtedly » or « there is no doubt », so the loss is regarded as certain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi say the losers are those cheated of their share of God's honour; Ibn Kathir adds that they lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi state that they squandered their lives on what leads only to everlasting punishment.

The exegetes agree that this fate results from their preference for the worldly life and their turning away from guidance, with the sealing of hearts, hearing and sight presented as a consequence of that turning away. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan distinguish between disbelief spoken by the tongue and disbelief held in the heart: the person compelled to speak while his heart remains firm in faith is not included in this threat. Al-Razi reports that most commentators link the revelation to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya finds this attribution weak given his high rank and sees the verse as applying rather to those who repented.

They also differ on the reading of « futinu »: most read it in the passive, Ibn 'Amir in the active, and opinions vary on who is meant by the migration and struggle that follow the trial. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

This verse states that after speaking of the one who disbelieves after faith, God turns to those who emigrated after being tried, then struggled and persevered: your Lord is forgiving and merciful to them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators understand the trial as torture and coercion into uttering words of disbelief while the heart remained firm in faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that God's being 'for them' means He is their protector and helper, not their enemy. The reader Ibn 'Amir reads the verb in the active form, which can mean that they tried themselves by outward concealment, or that they tempted other Muslims; the majority reading is the passive. Commentators differ on who is meant: al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi report several views, some referring to Muslims left in Mecca who later joined Medina, others naming 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a or al-Walid ibn al-Walid as transmitted by Ibn Ishaq. Ibn 'Atiyya considers mentioning 'Ammar unsuitable given his higher rank, while Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that it also concerns 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, who apostatised and then repented. Al-Razi stresses that real compulsion is needed to excuse an utterance of disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur notes that 'thumma' marks the distance in rank between these believers and those who remain in disbelief, and that the emigration may refer to the flight to Abyssinia. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that patience turns the trial into a purification from sins.

This verse describes the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself and every soul is repaid in full for what it did, without any wrong. Most commentators explain that on that Day each person will be absorbed in his own fate, crying out 'myself, myself'. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand the pleading as each soul defending itself by its deeds, good or bad, or offering excuses, like the people of the Fire who say, 'By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.' Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi read it the same way, and Ibn Kathir stresses that no one can plead for another, not even a father or a son. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy mention a different view: for some, the cry 'myself, myself' is not an argument at all but a mere longing, and Ibn Atiyya holds that the verse covers believers and disbelievers alike, while disbelievers may be silenced at other moments. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi transmit a report from Ka'b al-Ahbar about the roar of Hell and Abraham's cry for himself, and a report from Ibn Abbas about a dispute between soul and body illustrated by a blind man and a lame man, though al-Alusi doubts that report. On grammar, al-Tabari notes that the feminine verb agrees with nafs, some grammarians explaining it by the sense of 'each person' and others calling it an error. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari distinguish the first nafs as the whole person from the second as the self itself. The verse ends by confirming perfect justice: no one is wronged, neither by extra punishment nor by lost reward.

This verse offers a parable: a town that enjoyed security and peace, where its provision came abundantly from every direction, became ungrateful for God's blessings, and so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear as a consequence of its deeds. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, identify the town as Mecca and its people, who were not raided and to whom the produce of all things was brought. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the ingratitude was rejecting the Prophet, that the hunger lasted seven years until they ate al-'Ilhiz and carrion after his supplication, and that the fear came from the Prophet's expeditions surrounding them. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand ingratitude as failing to give thanks and obey, and note that the parable may refer to an unnamed town; al-Razi even judges that the town meant is probably not Mecca itself but another town used as an example for it. A different view, reported through Hafsa in al-Tabari's chain and by Ibn al-Jawzi, identifies the town as Medina at the time of 'Uthman's killing; Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Samʿani and al-Suyuti consider this weak or merely illustrative, and several hold it is a general parable for any such town. Readers differ on 'wal-khawf': most read it in the genitive, coordinated with hunger, while Abu 'Amr reads it in the accusative, coordinated with the garment. All agree that 'making it taste' and 'garment' are metaphors, with hunger and fear enveloping the body like clothing. The passage warns against ingratitude for God's blessings and against rejecting the messenger.

This verse states that a messenger from among the people of the town itself, whose lineage and truthfulness they knew, came to them, that they denied him, and that the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers, meaning polytheists who were ungrateful for God's blessings. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify the town as Mecca and the messenger as the Prophet Muhammad, and read the punishment as the famine that he invoked against them, with al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mentioning the killing of their leaders at Badr. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi transmit this reading, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that the town is not named and that the parable warns Mecca and all other towns until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari reports a narration from Hafsa, the Prophet's wife, who said the town was Medina; Ibn 'Atiyya explains that she meant Medina had fallen into the same danger the parable warns of. Al-Shawkani prefers the general reading, since the indefinite word for town gives it universality. The commentators agree that the next verse turns to the believers, commanding them to eat the lawful provision and give thanks, with the particle fa linking the two. They also explain that the phrase 'garment of hunger and fear' is a metaphor, which al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari analyse at length, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the punishment as a general one.

The verse tells believers to eat what God has provided, lawful and good, and to thank Him for His blessing, if they truly worship Him alone. Ibn Kathir explains that God alone grants provision and therefore alone deserves worship, and that the lawful is set against what harms people in their religion and their lives. Ibn Sa'di adds that food must be lawful and good, neither forbidden nor taken by usurpation, and enjoyed without excess; gratitude means acknowledging the blessing in the heart, praising God, and using His gifts in obedience. Al-Baydawi and al-Jaza'iri make this thanks practical: worship of God and abstention from what He has forbidden. Al-Zamakhshari reads the conditional phrase as meaning 'if you obey Him', or, if your claim is true, 'if you worship God through the idols you take as intercessors'. The commentators differ mainly on who is addressed. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that most hold it to be the Muslims. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, following Ibn 'Abbas, take the food to be war spoils, and al-Razi links the hunger in the preceding parable to disbelief, so that once they abandon unbelief they may eat. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Sha'rawi transmit another view, that the Prophet sent food to hungry Meccan polytheists; al-Tabari considers this far-fetched, since the following verses concern forbidden meats. Ibn 'Atiyya understands 'good' as 'pleasant', or as an emphasis on 'lawful'. Ibn 'Ashur suggests the address may concern the Muslims who emigrated to Abyssinia, and al-Alusi notes a view that it addresses the people of Medina, warned by Mecca's example.

This verse states that God has forbidden only four things as food: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God. Whoever is compelled by necessity, without desiring disobedience or exceeding what necessity requires, incurs no sin, for God is forgiving and merciful. The commentators agree that this ruling reflects the ease of the religion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that carrion means an animal that died of its own accord, and that the verse repeats what appears in Surat al-Baqara. Al-Razi notes that the restriction to these four prohibitions is affirmed in both Meccan and Medinan surahs. On the phrase "neither desiring nor transgressing," opinions differ. The majority, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi, take it to mean consuming these items while other food is available, or going beyond the limits God set. Others understand desiring as rebellion against the ruler or highway robbery, and transgressing as eating beyond what keeps one alive. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that Malik permitted eating to satiety and taking provisions. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to the rejection of prohibitions invented by the polytheists. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi identify the town in the preceding parable as Mecca, while Abu Hayyan lists several other readings. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi see the restriction as serving to distinguish the pure from the impure.

This verse forbids anyone from declaring something lawful or unlawful merely by what the tongue utters, saying 'this is lawful and this is unlawful' on their own authority, because such a claim is an invention against God, and those who invent lies against God do not prosper. The commentators explain that it first addressed the pagan Arabs who forbade the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham, and who claimed that what was in the bellies of livestock was reserved for their males. Ibn Kathir, al-Samʿani and al-Baghawi take it as a general rule covering anyone who institutes a prohibition or permission without a textual basis. All agree that the lie consists in attributing to God a ruling He did not give. Their enjoyment in this world is brief, and their painful punishment awaits them in the next, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn.

The scholars differ mainly on the grammar. Al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj hold that 'ma' is a verbal noun and that 'al-kadhib' is the object of 'taqulu'. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by Ibn Ashur, reads the lam in 'li-taftaru' as a lam of consequence rather than purpose: the fabrication results from their words without being their aim. Al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan consider a purposive meaning more apparent, since the people did attribute their own customs to God, as in verse 137 of al-An'am. Several recitations of 'al-kadhib' are also noted, as a complement, a qualifier or a plural, without changing the overall sense.

Some scholars draw from the verse a caution in issuing rulings. Abu Nadra said he feared giving fatwas since he heard this passage, and Malik, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Arabi, disliked a mufti saying 'this is lawful and this is unlawful' in matters of independent reasoning, preferring 'I dislike this'. Ibn Ashur clarifies that the blame falls on turning the lawful into the unlawful, not on abstaining from a food out of distaste.

The commentators explain that « a little enjoyment » is the predicate of an implied subject: whatever the people who fabricate lies against God gain is brief and slight in this world, and after it lies a painful punishment in the next. Most agree that the verse addresses pagans who declared things lawful or unlawful on their own authority while claiming God had commanded it, such as the bahira and the sa'iba. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report this sense, and Ibn Kathir extends it to anyone who innovates or forbids without a legal basis, by mere opinion. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud take the enjoyment to be the benefit of the practices of the Jahiliyya, while Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur understand it as the pleasure of this life. Ibn 'Atiyya explains that success (falah) may mean survival or the attainment of one's aims. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur read the lam in « li-taftaru » as the lam of consequence rather than purpose. Grammarians differ on the case of « al-kadhib »: it is the object of « taqulu » or of « tasifu » according to different readings, and some read it in the genitive or nominative. Al-Qurtubi relates that Malik and al-Nakha'i avoided saying « this is lawful, this is unlawful » in matters of interpretation, preferring to express dislike. The verse thus reminds that declaring something lawful or unlawful without proof is to lie about God.

This verse explains that the prohibitions placed on the Jews, which deprived them of certain good things, were a punishment, and that God did not wrong them by imposing them; they wronged themselves through rebellion and transgression. The commentators agree that the prohibitions referred to are those mentioned in Surat al-An'am: every animal with undivided hooves, and the fat of cattle and sheep except what their backs or intestines carry or what is mixed with bone, as al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Qatada report. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi see these as a punishment for their transgression, and their wrongdoing as their disobedience. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the verse as a warning against the polytheists' invented prohibitions, showing that the Jewish law itself contained restrictions specific to the Jews. Ibn 'Ashur notes that these prohibitions were not part of Abraham's law. Al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi state that this was a punishment specific to the Jews, since the things were lawful in themselves for others. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud see in it a distinction between this community and others, since for Muslims only what is harmful is forbidden. The verse continues with the forgiveness granted to one who does wrong out of ignorance, then repents and reforms. Most understand ignorance as not grasping the gravity of the sin, or desire overpowering judgment, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes it to mean deliberate defiance. None of these commentaries disputes that the responsibility for the harm rests with the Jews themselves.

This verse states that God forgives and shows mercy to those who do evil out of ignorance, then repent and mend their conduct. Al-Tabari explains that these are people who disobeyed God without reflecting on what they were doing, then returned to obedience through regret, repentance and seeking forgiveness. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: ignorance that the act is evil, or knowing it is evil yet being overcome by desire, and he adds a third, of someone who rushes into sin while promising himself to repent later. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi describe the ignorance as failing to reflect on the consequences because desire has overwhelmed reason. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that here ignorance is not the opposite of knowledge but stubborn transgression, though true ignorance often accompanies such acts. Ibn Kathir cites an early scholar saying that whoever disobeys God is ignorant. All agree that reform means persisting in repentance and abandoning the sin. The phrase 'after it' refers to the repentance according to most, though some take it to mean the ignorance or the sin. Al-Qurtubi reports from Ibn 'Abbas that evil here means associating partners with God, while most extend the meaning to every sin. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as reassurance for Muslims after the rebuke of idolatrous practices.

In this verse God praises His friend Abraham, describing him as a whole community in himself, meaning a model of goodness who is followed, devoted and obedient to God, inclined toward the true religion, and never one of the polytheists. The commentators see in this a reply to the Quraysh, who claimed to follow Abraham's faith, and to the Jews and Christians, who also claimed him.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report at length the explanation of Ibn Mas'ud: the community is one who teaches good, and the devout one is one who obeys God and His Messenger. Mujahid understood that Abraham alone was a believer among a world of unbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi held that he combined qualities usually found only scattered among many people, a view followed by al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi list several meanings for the other terms: the devout one is obedient, or persistent in worship, or frequent in supplication; the one who inclines toward the true faith is sincere according to Muqatil, or a pilgrim according to al-Kalbi.

The commentators give several readings of the blessing bestowed in this world: a good reputation and a tongue of truth (Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid), prophethood (al-Hasan), acceptance by all religious communities (Qatada), or a righteous offspring. Several of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Shawkani, note that these meanings do not exclude one another.

The following verse commands the Prophet to follow the religion of Abraham, and the commentators differ on its scope: following everything not abrogated, or only the core beliefs such as rejecting idols and submitting to God, as al-Tabari holds. Al-Qurtubi judges that doctrine takes precedence over legal rules, while others point to the rites of pilgrimage.

This verse describes Abraham as a model to follow, a man who embodied all the qualities of goodness, devoted to obedience to God, turning away from falsehood toward truth, free from any association with others in worship, and grateful for his Lord's favours. God chose him, favoured him, and guided him to the straight path, which is the religion of Islam based on pure monotheism. The commentators agree that these qualities show he was not what the Quraysh, the Jews, or the Christians claimed by affiliating themselves with him. They also agree that the word "ummah" here refers to a person who is worth a whole community, or to a leader one follows. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Mas'ud report that it means one who teaches good, while al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya cite other meanings, such as a man who alone believed in his time according to Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain his singular standing by his complete perfection in these virtues, and they note the verse's emphasis on gratitude, which the Quraysh failed to show.

Verse 16:122 describes the honour God gave Abraham in this world and his standing in the next. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: he was granted a good state in this life, and in the Hereafter he is counted among the righteous. They differ mainly on what the good granted in this world refers to. Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi understand it as a true tongue of honesty, a good mention that lasts through the ages. Qatada, reported by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, holds that all religious communities accept and honour him, while Ibn Atiyya sees it as his leadership over all creation. Al-Hasan, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean prophethood, whereas Muqatil ibn Hayyan, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi relate it to the prayer upon him that Muslims recite in the tashahhud. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Shinqiti mention righteous descendants, and al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di combine these honours with provision, health and a good life. On the Hereafter, al-Baghawi says he will be among the righteous with his righteous forefathers in Paradise, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi say he will be among the people of Paradise. Al-Razi notes that this phrase does not exclude the highest ranks of the righteous, and he links it to Abraham's prayer in Surah al-Shu'ara'. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that the reward given in this life is not the full recompense, which belongs to the Hereafter, and al-Sha'rawi agrees that the reward of the Hereafter is greater.

In this verse God commands His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to follow the religion of Abraham, as a pure monotheist (hanif) who turns away from false creeds, and states that Abraham was not among the idolaters. The commentators generally understand the word millah here as the foundations of faith: monotheism, rejection of idols and submission to God. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this following concerns the principles of belief rather than the practical rules that change with time. Others, as reported by al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy, take it to include all of Abraham's law except what was abrogated, and al-Mawardi cites a Shafi'i current that holds the same view; Ibn 'Ashur reads it as agreement with the principles of human nature. Al-Sam'ani and al-Razi draw from the verse that a superior may follow an inferior, while Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan stress that the Prophet ﷺ is the most excellent of messengers. On the term hanif, al-Tabari explains it as one who turns away from idols, Ibn 'Atiyya as one who inclines toward good, and al-Razi notes that it also refers to circumcision and pilgrimage. The following verses about the Sabbath are explained by the commentators as not being part of Abraham's religion; it was imposed on those who disagreed about it, and they agree that God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.

This verse states that the Sabbath was imposed on those who disagreed about it, which most commentators identify as the Jews, and that God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they differed over. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di agree that the Sabbath was not part of the religion of Abraham.

The commentators differ on the nature of the disagreement. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report, through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi, that Moses ordered them to honour Friday, but they chose Saturday because God finished creation on that day, so the Sabbath was imposed on them. Al-Tabari also cites Ibn Zayd for the view that they abandoned Friday for another day. Al-Mawardi lists three opinions, and al-Sam'ani reads the Sabbath as a curse upon them.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan offer a different reading, in which the dispute concerned hunting: they sometimes allowed it on the Sabbath and sometimes forbade it, so the punishment, their transformation into apes, fell upon them. Qatada is cited as saying that some considered it lawful and others forbidden.

Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi stress that the verse concerns opposition to the prophets rather than disagreement among the Jews, and that it answers the Jewish claim to Abraham's religion. Al-Qurtubi relies on the hadith of Abu Hurayra, which assigns Friday to this community, to argue that God had not specified the day for them. The verse closes with a warning that God will reward and punish each party according to what it deserves.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to invite people to the way of his Lord, meaning Islam, with wisdom, which is the sound argument that makes the truth clear and removes doubt, and with fair exhortation, made of admonitions, lessons, encouragement and warning. He is also to dispute with those who oppose him in the best manner, gently and without harshness. The verse ends by affirming that God knows best who strays from His way and who is guided, so the Prophet's duty is only to convey the message. The commentators agree that wisdom refers to the Quran or to a conclusive proof, that fair exhortation means the Quran's admonitions and its commands and prohibitions joined with hope and fear, and that the best dispute means being gentle and avoiding insult. On the ruling, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Nahhas and Ibn Zayd hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, while the majority, including al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, consider it still valid for disobedient believers and for those whose faith may be hoped for without fighting. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report an occasion linked to the battle of Uhud and the mutilation of Hamza, though most treat the verse as Meccan and connected to what precedes it. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya link the three methods to the levels of people: the elite by demonstration, the common folk by exhortation, and the stubborn by the finest argument. Ibn al-Qayyim regards this as the correct meaning.

This verse permits a person who has been wronged to retaliate against the wrongdoer with a punishment equal to what was inflicted, without exceeding it, and states that patience in refraining is better for those who are patient. The commentators differ on its occasion of revelation and its legal scope. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, report that it was revealed concerning the dead of Uhud, whose bodies were mutilated, especially Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib. The Muslims then vowed to do the same if they prevailed, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, refrained and made expiation for his oath. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd hold that it was abrogated by the verses on fighting, whereas Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, al-Nakha'i and al-Thawri consider it muhkam and general in meaning, forbidding the victim to take more than he suffered. Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabari see no proof of abrogation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress equivalence in kind and measure. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi record a disagreement over whether a victim may take back from a trust held by the one who wronged him: Ibn Sirin and Mujahid allow it, while Malik forbids it, citing the hadith «Return the trust to the one who entrusted you». Ibn Ashur notes that the first act is called a punishment by verbal parallelism. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses at length the greater merit of patience, while most commentators agree that retaliation is permitted but restraint is better, the verse addressing believers and the Prophet with them.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to be patient in the face of the harm inflicted by the disbelievers, and the commentators agree that such patience can only come through God's help and support. The prohibition against grieving over them and against being constricted by their scheming is explained by many as meaning that his heart should not be straitened on their account. Most report that the patience intended is refraining from retaliating in kind and from mutilating enemies, as had been done to the martyrs of Uhud, especially Hamza. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the grief to concern the disbelievers, while al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also allow that it may refer to the Uhud dead. All note that God being with those who are mindful and those who do good means His help, support and protection. On the reading of ḍayq, al-Tabari prefers the fatha form, Ibn Kathir reads it with kasra, and grammarians such as Abu 'Ubayda distinguish between inner distress and material narrowness, while al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba treat the two as equivalent forms. Al-Razi analyses the sources of anger as the loss of a past benefit and the fear of a future harm, seeing the verse as addressing both. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd consider the command to patience abrogated by the verses on fighting, while the majority hold it to be still in force.

This verse states that God is with those who are mindful of Him by avoiding what He forbids, and with those who do good by fulfilling their obligations and doing beautiful deeds. The commentators understand this divine companionship as support, help, aid and success granted to the believers, not as the general presence of knowledge that encompasses all creatures. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Sa'di explain that piety means abstaining from prohibitions, while ihsan means performing the obligations and acts of obedience. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the verse concludes the preceding verses on justice, patience and calling people with wisdom, and provides their justification. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari distinguish this special companionship from the general presence of God's knowledge, hearing and sight. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand piety as reverence for God's command and ihsan as compassion toward His creatures. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur observe that the first clause is in the past tense to mark the acquisition of piety, and the second is nominal to mark the constancy of ihsan. Al-Sha'rawi sees ihsan as going beyond what is required, citing the hadith of Gabriel. Regarding the neighbouring verses, some scholars hold that they were abrogated by the verse of fighting, while most treat them as valid.
